title: Probability & Statistics: The Big Picture
objective: After this level you can explain the two big jobs of this tree: describing many cases with a few numbers, and measuring how likely things are.
summary: Statistics describes many cases with a few numbers; probability measures how likely things are. Both began in the 1600s, with Graunt's death lists and Pascal and Fermat's letters.

cards.headline: In the 1600s, a tradesman and two mathematicians started this whole tree.
cards.body: One summed up London's lists of the dead. The other two swapped letters about a game of chance that never finished. Between them, they set up the two big jobs you'll learn to do here.

cards.headline: Job 1: describe many cases with a few numbers
cards.body: London published its Bills of Mortality every week: christenings, burials and causes of death, parish by parish. In 1662 John Graunt, a London tradesman, added them up and hunted for patterns. One stood out: for every 14 boys christened, about 13 girls were, again and again. A pile of weekly lists became one short ratio. That's statistics: collecting data and summing it up so you can see what it says.

cards.headline: Job 2: measure how likely
cards.body: In the summer of 1654, Blaise Pascal and Pierre de Fermat traded letters about a puzzle. Two players stop a game of chance before anyone has won. How should they split the pot fairly? Working it out, they laid the foundation of probability: the mathematics of how likely something is to happen. Not bad for an argument about an unfinished game.

mascot.line: If you remember one thing from this level: statistics describes, probability measures chance.

cards.fact: Statistics describes what the data say. Probability measures chance.
cards.context: Summing up a pile of data is descriptive statistics, Graunt's job. Asking how likely an event is belongs to probability, Pascal and Fermat's job. Every level in this tree does one or both, and both run on everyday tools like percentages, rates and big numbers. That's where Chapter 1 goes next.

title: What a Percent Really Is
objective: After this level you can turn "3 out of 20" into a percentage and explain that percent simply means "out of every 100".
summary: Percent means "by the hundred". To turn "3 out of 20" into a percent, divide (0.15) and move the decimal point: 15%. Percents put groups of different sizes on one scale.

cards.headline: "3 out of 20" and "15%" are the same number in different clothes.
cards.body: Percent can look like its own special kind of math. It isn't. It's a way of saying "out of every 100", and once you see that, you can turn any "out of" into a percent.

cards.headline: Percent means "by the hundred"
cards.body: The word comes from the Latin per centum, "by the hundred". It's the same hundred hiding in a century (100 years) and a cent (a hundredth of a dollar). So 15% simply means 15 out of every 100. A percent is a ratio whose bottom number is always 100, and that fixed bottom number is exactly what makes it handy.

cards.headline: Turning "out of" into a percent
cards.body: Say 3 of the 20 cupcakes on a tray are chocolate. Divide the part by the whole: 3 ÷ 20 = 0.15. Move the decimal point two places right and you get 15%. Another way to see it: scale the tray up five times and you'd have 100 cupcakes, 15 of them chocolate. Same share, now "out of 100".

cards.fact: Percents let you compare groups of different sizes.
cards.context: Which tray is more chocolate: 3 out of 20, or 12 out of 100? The raw counts say the second, since 12 beats 3. Percents say the first: 15% beats 12%. Putting everything "out of 100" puts big and small groups on the same footing, a trick this chapter keeps using.

title: Percent Change
objective: After this level you can work out how much something rose or fell in percent by comparing the change with where it started.
summary: Percent change is the change divided by the starting value. A $5 rise is 25% on a $20 ticket but only 1% on a $500 phone, and a fall from $25 to $20 is 20%.

cards.headline: A $20 ticket goes up $5. Is that a lot? It depends where you started.
cards.body: Five dollars on a $20 ticket feels steep. The same five dollars on a $500 phone barely registers. Percent change is the tool that tells those two apart.

cards.headline: Change divided by start
cards.body: To find a percent change, first find the change: new minus old. Then divide it by where you started, and turn the answer into a percent. The ticket went from $20 to $25, a change of $5. And 5 ÷ 20 = 0.25, so the price rose 25%.

cards.headline: Same $5, different story
cards.body: Now the phone: $500 up to $505. The change is still $5, but 5 ÷ 500 is just 0.01, a 1% rise. The starting value is the ruler you measure the change against. A small start makes a big percent; a big start makes a small one. So whenever you hear "up 25%", ask the follow-up: up from what?

cards.fact: Falling works the same way, measured from where the fall began.
cards.context: A $25 ticket cut back to $20 has dropped $5, and 5 ÷ 25 = 0.2: a 20% fall. Same $5 as the rise, but this time it's measured against $25, a bigger start, so the percent is smaller. Tuck that away. It's the whole secret of the next level.

title: Up 50%, Down 50%
objective: After this level you can explain why a 50% drop followed by a 50% rise leaves you worse off than where you began.
summary: A 50% fall and a 50% rise leave you 25% below where you began, in either order, because each percent is taken from a different starting value. Recovering from a 50% fall takes a 100% rise.

cards.headline: Your $100 drops 50%, then rises 50%. Back to $100, right?
cards.body: Nope. You end up with $75. No fees, no tricks, just arithmetic. Here's where the missing $25 went.

cards.headline: Each percent has its own starting point
cards.body: The first 50% is taken from $100, so you lose $50 and have $50 left. The second 50% is measured from that new, smaller start: half of $50 is only $25. Up $25 lands you at $75. Same percent, different base, so the fall and the rise aren't the same size in dollars. It's Level 3's "up from what?" twice in a row.

cards.headline: The order doesn't save you
cards.body: Flip it. Up 50% first: $100 becomes $150. Then down 50%: half of $150 is $75 gone, leaving $75 again. Whenever a rise and a fall of the same percent follow each other, the second one works on a different number, and you finish below the start. Even up 10% then down 10% turns $100 into $99.

cards.fact: After a 50% fall, you need a 100% rise to get back.
cards.context: From $50, climbing back to $100 means gaining another $50, and 50 ÷ 50 is 1, or 100%. The deeper the fall, the steeper the climb back. So when something "fell 50% and has bounced back 50%", you know it's still a quarter below where it started.

title: Percent vs. Percentage Points
objective: After this level you can tell a rise of 5 percentage points from a rise of 5 percent, and spot a headline that mixes them up.
summary: Going from 10% to 15% is a rise of 5 percentage points (subtract) and a 50 percent increase (divide by the start). Both are true; headlines often mix them up.

cards.headline: A share goes from 10% to 15%. Did it rise by 5 or by 50?
cards.body: Both answers are right, in different units. One counts percentage points; the other is a percent increase. Mix them up and a headline can make a change look far bigger or smaller than it is.

cards.headline: Points: just subtract
cards.body: When you compare two percentages, the plain difference is measured in percentage points. Say the share of students who walk to school goes from 10% to 15%. Subtract: 15 minus 10 is 5 percentage points. Points tell you how far the number moved on the scale from 0 to 100.

mascot.line: People mix these two up all the time. Points: subtract. Percent: divide by the start.

cards.headline: Percent: compare with the start
cards.body: Percent change uses Level 3's rule: change ÷ start. The change is 5 and the start is 10, and 5 ÷ 10 = 0.5, a 50% rise. Walkers really did grow by half: 10 in every 100 students became 15 in every 100. Both statements are true. They answer different questions.

cards.fact: "Percentage change and percentage-point change get mixed up all the time."
cards.context: That warning comes from Jennifer LaFleur, an editor quoted by The Journalist's Resource. The rule of thumb: when you compare two percentages, the difference is in percentage points. So a headline saying walkers are "up 5%" when the share went from 10% to 15% has undersold a 50% jump.

title: Rates: Counting Per Person
objective: After this level you can explain why comparing totals between a big place and a small one misleads, and why rates per person fix it.
summary: Totals mislead when places differ in size. A rate divides the count by the population, often per 100,000 people: a city with ten times the cases can have a tenth of the rate.

cards.headline: Big cities have more of almost everything. That alone tells you little.
cards.body: More people means more births, more bakeries and more broken legs. So when a big city beats a small town in some total, the first question is whether it simply has more people. Totals can't answer that.

cards.headline: Totals can't compare different sizes
cards.body: Picture a town of 10,000 people with 50 cases of flu, and a city of 1,000,000 people with 500 cases. The city has ten times as many cases. Sounds worse. But a total ignores how many people could have caught it. Counts don't take a population's size into account, so on their own they can't fairly compare places of different sizes.

cards.headline: Divide by the people
cards.body: A rate fixes that: divide the count by the population, then scale it to a round number of people. Health statisticians often use "per 100,000". The town: 50 cases among 10,000 people is 500 per 100,000. The city: 500 among 1,000,000 is just 50 per 100,000. The town's rate is ten times the city's. The comparison flipped.

cards.fact: A percent is a rate's little cousin.
cards.context: A percent is a rate per 100. Per 100,000 is the same idea with a bigger crowd, handy when events are rare. Either way, a rate answers the question a total can't: how common is this, person for person?

title: "1 in 3" Beats 33%
objective: After this level you can switch between percentages, fractions and "1 in N" counts, and explain why counts of people are easier to picture.
summary: "1 in N" is 100 ÷ N percent, so 1 in 4 is 25% and a bigger N means a smaller share. Simple counts like "2 in 5" are easier to picture than percents, especially with the same bottom number.

cards.headline: In the 1980s, a burger flopped because 3 looks smaller than 4.
cards.body: A&W sold a third-pound burger for the same price as McDonald's Quarter Pounder. More meat, same money. According to A. Alfred Taubman, A&W's owner at the time, focus groups asked why they should pay the same for less. Many thought a third was smaller than a quarter.

cards.headline: Three ways to say one share
cards.body: 1 in 4, one quarter and 25% are the same share. To turn "1 in N" into a percent, divide 100 by N: 1 in 4 is 25%, 1 in 5 is 20%, 1 in 3 is about 33%. To go back, divide 100 by the percent. And notice the twist that sank the burger: in "1 in N", a bigger N means a smaller share. A third (1 in 3) beats a quarter (1 in 4).

cards.headline: Counts of people are easier to picture
cards.body: Some studies suggest patients grasp simple counts, like "2 in 5", better than "40 percent". Same share, different picture. A percent is an abstract slice of a hundred; a count gives you people to imagine. Two people in a room of five is something your mind can actually see.

cards.fact: Best of all: counts with the same bottom number.
cards.context: Is 1 in 12 more than 1 in 17? It takes a moment. Put both over 50, about 4 in 50 against 3 in 50, and the answer is instant. Risk experts advise exactly that. They also warn that a lone "1 in X" can make a risk seem bigger than it is.

title: How Big Is a Billion?
objective: After this level you can picture the difference between a thousand, a million and a billion using seconds of time.
summary: A billion is a thousand millions. Counted in seconds, a thousand is about 17 minutes, a million about 11 and a half days, and a billion almost 32 years.

cards.headline: A million and a billion sound like neighbors. In seconds, they're decades apart.
cards.body: Our ears hear "million" and "billion" as one small step. Counting them out in seconds shows just how big that step is.

cards.headline: Each step is 1,000 times bigger
cards.body: A thousand is 1,000. A million is a thousand thousands. A billion is a thousand millions: 1,000,000,000. The metric prefixes climb the same ladder, with kilo for thousand, mega for million and giga for billion. Each rung multiplies by a thousand, which makes a billion a million times bigger than a thousand.

mascot.line: Don't memorize the exact days. Keep the picture: a million seconds is a vacation, a billion is decades.

cards.headline: Why it matters in the news
cards.body: A day has 86,400 seconds, so a million of them is gone in under two weeks. A billion takes almost 32 years. Next time a headline puts $5 million next to $5 billion, picture the seconds: a short vacation against three decades of birthdays. The billion isn't a bit bigger. It's 1,000 times bigger.

title: Too Precise to Be True
objective: After this level you can explain how a number can look more exact than the measurement behind it, using the 98.6 degree fever line.
summary: The 98.6°F fever-chart line comes from Wunderlich's round 37°C, converted to Fahrenheit. The decimal came from the formula, not a sharper thermometer; a 1992 study found an average of 98.2°F.

cards.headline: 98.6°F looks measured to a tenth of a degree. It never was.
cards.body: That famous line on fever charts goes back to a German doctor's book from 1868. His number was a round 37°C. The .6 turned up when someone converted it.

cards.headline: A huge study, a round number
cards.body: Carl Wunderlich reportedly analyzed over a million underarm readings from some 25,000 patients. The average he gave for healthy adults was 37°C. Written as 37, that's a number to the nearest whole degree: it could stand for anything from 36.5°C to 37.5°C. The digits you write down are a promise about how sharp the measuring was.

cards.headline: Where the .6 came from
cards.body: To turn Celsius into Fahrenheit, multiply by 1.8 and add 32. Do that to 37 and you get exactly 98.6. The decimal comes from the formula, not from a better thermometer, and a calculation can't make a number more precise than its measurement. That 36.5 to 37.5 range is 97.7°F to 99.5°F. Tellingly, NIST's table of everyday temperatures lists body temperature as 37°C and 99°F.

cards.fact: When researchers measured again in 1992, the average was 98.2°F.
cards.context: A University of Maryland team took 700 oral readings from 148 healthy adults. The average was 36.8°C (98.2°F), and exactly 98.6°F came up in only 56 of the 700 readings. A number's decimals only mean something if the measurement behind them was that sharp.

title: The Mean: Add Up and Share Out
objective: After this level you can find the mean of a set of numbers and explain it as the amount each would get if the total were shared equally.
summary: The mean adds up every value and divides by how many there are: the fair share each would get if the total were split equally. Per person figures are means.

cards.headline: Pour every glass into one jug, then share it out evenly.
cards.body: Each glass ends up with the same amount. That amount has a name you hear all the time, usually as "the average". This level shows what it really is.

mascot.line: If you remember one thing from this level: add them all up, then share equally. That is the mean.

cards.headline: Add up, then share out
cards.body: To find the mean, add up all the values, then divide by how many there are. Picture five bottles holding 1, 4, 2, 3 and 0 liters of water. Pour them together and you have 10 liters. Share that equally among the 5 bottles and each gets 2 liters. So the mean is 2 liters, even though only one bottle held exactly that to begin with.

cards.headline: A fair share nobody has to own
cards.body: That is the best way to picture a mean: the fair share each member would get if everything were pooled and split evenly. It works for anything you can add. Quiz scores of 70, 90, 86 and 94 total 340; shared over 4 quizzes, that is 85 each. Not one quiz actually scored 85, and that is fine. The mean is not a value picked from the list. It is the level everything would settle at if you evened it out.

cards.fact: "Average" usually means the mean, and it counts every value.
cards.context: The two words are used interchangeably, and the mean is the most common way to describe a center. Per capita income is a mean: all the income in a place, divided among every man, woman and child. That is Level 6's move of dividing by the population. And because the mean counts every value, one huge value can move it. Level 13 shows how far.

title: The Median: The Middle One
objective: After this level you can find the median by lining values up in order and explain why it is the "typical" middle case.
summary: The median is the middle value once the data are lined up in order, with half on each side. With an even count, it is halfway between the two middle values.

cards.headline: Line people up by age and point at the one in the middle.
cards.body: No adding, no dividing. You have just found another kind of average, and it answers a different question from the mean: not "what is the fair share?" but "who is in the middle?"

cards.headline: Order first, then find the middle
cards.body: The median is the middle value once everything is lined up in order. Take the retirement ages of 11 people, lined up from 54 to 60. Count in from either end and the sixth age, 57, sits in the middle, with five ages below it and five above. That is the whole idea: half the list on each side.

cards.headline: An even count? Split the difference
cards.body: With an even number of values there is no single middle, so take the two middle ones and find their mean. Add a twelfth person who retired at 52, and the two middle ages become 56 and 57. The median is halfway between them: 56.5. It is fine for a median to be a value nobody in the list has.

cards.fact: Half above, half below: that is what makes the median typical.
cards.context: The median does not add anything up; it just needs the values in order, so it describes the middle case. For those 11 retirement ages, the ages add up to 623 and the mean is about 56.6, close to the median of 57. When mean and median agree like that, either works. When they do not, the gap tells a story. That is next level.

title: When Mean and Median Disagree
objective: After this level you can explain why a few very large values pull the mean far above the median, as with incomes and house prices.
summary: A few very large values pull the mean far above the median. In 2024, US median household income was $83,730; the mean was $121,000.

cards.headline: Nine friends earn $50,000. A tenth earns $1,050,000. What's typical?
cards.body: Ask the mean and the answer is $150,000, a salary nine of the ten would love to have. Ask the median and you get $50,000. Same ten people, two very different stories.

cards.headline: One big value drags the mean
cards.body: The total pay is $1,500,000. Shared over ten people, the mean is $150,000, three times what nine of them earn. The median does not care how big the top value is. Line the ten up and the two in the middle both earn $50,000, so the median stays put. The mean counts every value, so outliers pull it; the median only needs the middle.

cards.headline: Long tails pull the mean
cards.body: Incomes look like that friend group, only bigger: most people bunch lower down, and a long tail of high earners stretches off to the right. In a lopsided, or skewed, set like this, the mean gets pulled toward the tail, and most values, the median included, sit below it. House prices can work the same way: one mansion on the street lifts the mean price, not the median.

mascot.line: Common mix-up: "the average household" can mean either one. With income, the gap is tens of thousands of dollars.

cards.fact: In 2024, US median household income was $83,730. The mean was $121,000.
cards.context: The Census Bureau's median splits households into two equal halves: half had more income, half less. The mean sits about $37,000 higher, lifted by the top incomes. So for lopsided numbers like income, the median is usually the better guide to what is typical. When someone quotes an "average", ask which one.

title: The Mode: Most Popular Wins
objective: After this level you can find the mode and explain when the most common value is the most useful average, as with shoe sizes.
summary: The mode is the most common value. It is the only average that works for categories like colors, and it suits questions like which shoe size to stock.

cards.headline: A shoe shop doesn't want the average size. It wants the size people buy.
cards.body: Stocking up on the mean would be a strange plan. The shop needs a third kind of average: the one that simply counts which value turns up most.

cards.headline: The most common value
cards.body: The mode is the value that appears most often. Say five customers wear sizes 6, 7, 7, 7 and 11. The mode is 7: three of the five wear it. The mean is 38 ÷ 5 = 7.6, a size nobody in the group wears. For deciding which boxes to order, the mode is the average that fits.

cards.headline: The only average for words
cards.body: Ask a class for favorite colors: red, red, red, green, green, yellow, purple, black, blue. You cannot add colors, and you cannot line them up from small to large, so there is no mean and no median. But you can count them, and red wins. Of the three averages, only the mode works for categories like colors.

title: Outliers
objective: After this level you can spot an outlier and decide whether it is a mistake to fix or a real case worth keeping.
summary: An outlier sits far from the rest and can pull the mean. Investigate it: a proven mistake is corrected or removed; a real case, like Robert Wadlow's 272 cm, is kept.

cards.headline: A height survey lists someone at 272 cm. Typo, or record?
cards.body: It could be a slip of the keyboard. Or it could be Robert Wadlow, measured at 272 cm in 1940. Values that stand far from the rest are called outliers, and the job is working out which kind you have found.

cards.headline: Far from the rest
cards.body: An outlier is a value notably different from the rest of the data, and it matters because it can bend your results. Swap one retirement age of 60 for 81 in Level 12's list of 11, and the mean jumps from about 56.6 to about 58.5. The median? Still 57. Before you trust any average, look for values sitting far out on their own.

cards.headline: A mistake? Fix it
cards.body: Some outliers are simply bad data: a number typed wrong, an experiment run incorrectly. If a survey of schoolchildren lists a child aged 123, somebody slipped. When a value is shown to be an error, you correct it if you can, or take it out.

mascot.line: If you remember one thing: investigate an outlier before you touch it. Mistakes get fixed; real cases stay.

cards.headline: Real? Keep it
cards.body: Other outliers are true. Wadlow really was 272 cm (8 ft 11.1 in), the tallest man in medical history with irrefutable evidence. Deleting him would make the data tidier and wrong. That is why outliers get investigated before anyone touches them, and are not deleted just for being inconvenient. A real outlier can be the most interesting value you have.

title: Same Average, Different Spread
objective: After this level you can explain why two sets with the same average can be very different, and measure the gap with the range.
summary: Two sets can share an average yet differ in spread. The range, largest minus smallest, measures it quickly, but it uses only two values.

cards.headline: Two classes both average 70 on a test. Are they the same?
cards.body: In one, the scores were 40, 70 and 100. In the other, 69, 70 and 71. Same mean, very different rooms.

cards.headline: The average isn't the whole story
cards.body: In the first class, one student scored 30 below the mean and another 30 above it. In the second, everyone sat within a point of 70. The mean cannot tell those rooms apart. That is why a good summary also reports how spread out the values are: two sets can share a mean and still look nothing alike.

cards.headline: The range: biggest minus smallest
cards.body: The simplest measure of spread is the range: subtract the smallest value from the largest. First class: 100 − 40 = 60 points. Second class: 71 − 69 = 2 points. One more number, and suddenly the two rooms look as different as they really are.

cards.fact: The range looks at only two values.
cards.context: It uses just the largest and the smallest and ignores everything in between. So a single outlier at either end can stretch it, even if every other value sits tight. Handy for a quick look; for a fuller picture you need a measure that listens to every value. That is next level.

title: Spread in One Number
objective: After this level you can explain the standard deviation in plain words as the typical distance of values from the average.
summary: The standard deviation is a typical distance of values from the mean, built from every value: small when values bunch together, large when they scatter.

cards.headline: The range listens to two values. Can one number listen to all of them?
cards.body: Yes, and you have probably seen its name in a report: the standard deviation. Karl Pearson gave it that name. You will not calculate it here; you just need to know what it is telling you.

cards.headline: How far from the average, typically
cards.body: The standard deviation measures how far values sit from their mean. Think of it as a typical distance from the average. Unlike the range, it takes every value into account, asking how close each one is to the mean. It also comes in the same units as the data: measure in minutes, and it comes out in minutes.

cards.headline: Small means tight, big means scattered
cards.body: Take two sets that both have a mean of 6. In one, the values run from 4 to 8, mostly 5s, 6s and 7s; its standard deviation is about 1. In the other, they run from 1 to 11, and it is about 3. Same center, three times the typical distance. If every value were identical, the standard deviation would be zero.

cards.fact: Karl Pearson named it the standard deviation in 1893.
cards.context: He used the term in a lecture and put it in print in 1894, replacing older names such as "mean error". The idea itself was already nearly a century old. What stuck was the name, and now a report can say in one number how spread out its data are.

title: The Bell Curve
objective: After this level you can describe the bell curve, where most values bunch near the middle, and name everyday measurements that follow it.
summary: In a bell curve most values bunch near the middle and thin out evenly on both sides. About 68% sit within one standard deviation of the mean, about 95% within two.

cards.headline: Line up 5,738 soldiers' chest sizes and a bell appears.
cards.body: In 1846 the Belgian scholar Adolphe Quetelet did roughly that with old army records. The shape he showed off turns up again and again in measurements of people, and it has a name: the bell curve.

cards.headline: Most in the middle, fewer at the edges
cards.body: The records came from Scottish militiamen. The most common chest sizes were 39 and 40 inches, with more than 1,000 men each. Step away from the middle in either direction and the counts shrink steadily, down to a handful at 33 and 48 inches. Draw it as a bar chart and you get a hump in the middle with tails on both sides: a bell.

cards.headline: The shape of the bell
cards.body: A bell curve is symmetrical: its left half mirrors its right. So the mean, median and mode all land together, right in the middle. Heights within one sex come close to this shape, and so do most IQ scores. But not everything is bell-shaped. Level 13's incomes have a long tail on one side, which is exactly why their mean and median split apart.

mascot.line: Don't memorize 99.7. Keep 68 and 95: about two-thirds within one step, nearly all within two.

cards.fact: About 68% of values fall within one standard deviation of the mean.
cards.context: About 95% fall within two, and about 99.7% within three. In a textbook example, boys aged 15 to 18 in Chile in 2009 to 2010 averaged 170 cm, with a standard deviation of about 6 cm. So roughly two-thirds were between about 164 and 176 cm. On a bell curve, the standard deviation tells you how unusual a value is.

title: Percentiles

cards.headline: "Your child is in the 90th percentile." That's not a score out of 100.
cards.body: It is not a grade at all. It is a position in a line of other children, and once you picture the line, the number makes sense.

cards.headline: Your place in a line of 100

cards.headline: What a growth chart is saying

On the CDC's charts, a 5-year-old girl at the 25th percentile for weight weighs the same as or more than 25% of 5-year-old girls, and less than the other 75%. It is a position, not a verdict: the chart says where she stands in the line.

title: What a Probability Is
objective: After this level you can place a chance on the scale from impossible (0) to certain (1) and explain it as a long-run share of outcomes.
summary: A probability is a number from 0 (never) to 1 (always). It describes the long run, the share of times something happens over many tries, and for equally likely outcomes you count and divide.

cards.headline: A coin has a 1 in 2 chance of heads. So what will the next flip be?
cards.body: Nobody knows, and nobody can. A probability doesn't predict one flip. It tells you something sturdier, about what happens when you flip again and again. This level shows what that number really measures.

cards.headline: Every chance lives between 0 and 1
cards.body: Probabilities run on a scale from 0 to 1. A 0 means the event never happens, like rolling a 7 on one ordinary die, whose faces only go from 1 to 6. A 1 means it always happens. Halfway, 0.5 means it's as likely to happen as not. Chapter 1's tools still work here: 0.5 is 50%, or 1 in 2. The closer to 1, the likelier the event.

cards.headline: A probability is a long-run share
cards.body: So what does 0.5 promise for a coin? Not the next flip. It describes the long run: flip a fair coin 20 times, then 2,000, then 20,000, and the share of heads creeps closer and closer to 0.5. That's how statisticians define it: the probability of an outcome is its long-term relative frequency. One flip is a surprise. Twenty thousand flips are a pattern.

cards.fact: When outcomes are equally likely, count them.
cards.context: A fair die's six faces are equally likely. What's the chance of rolling at least 5? Two faces (5 and 6) out of six, so 2 in 6, which is 1 in 3. Count the outcomes you want, divide by all the outcomes, and you have a probability. That simple rule powers the next few levels.

title: Counting the Outcomes
objective: After this level you can list the equally likely outcomes of two dice and explain why 7 is the most common total.
summary: Galileo explained why three dice make 10 more often than 9 by counting throws, not sums. Two dice give 36 equally likely throws; 7 is made six ways (1 in 6), while 2 and 12 have one way each.

cards.headline: Dice players in Galileo's day noticed that three dice made 10 more often than 9.
cards.body: It seemed wrong. Each total can be built from six different sets of numbers. Galileo was asked to explain it, and his answer is the trick behind every dice chance: count the throws, not the sums.

cards.headline: Galileo counted throws, not sums
cards.body: Galileo's key move was to treat the dice as separate. One die can land 6 ways. Add a second, and each of its faces pairs with each face of the first: 6 × 6 = 36 throws. A third die makes 216. Counted that way, a total of 10 turns up in 27 of the throws and 9 in only 25. The players' long observation had been right all along; now it had a reason.

cards.headline: Two dice, 36 equal throws
cards.body: Now just two dice. Imagine one red and one blue, so a red 2 with a blue 5 is a different throw from a red 5 with a blue 2. That gives 36 equally likely throws. A total of 7 can be made six ways: 1 and 6, 2 and 5, 3 and 4, each either way round. A total of 2 needs both dice on 1, and 12 needs double 6: one way each.

mascot.line: Common mix-up: the totals are not equally likely, the throws are. Count the 36 throws first, then sort them into totals.

cards.fact: 7 comes up 1 time in 6. Snake eyes, 1 time in 36.
cards.context: Six of the 36 throws make 7, so its chance is 6 in 36, or 1 in 6: better than any other total. A 2 (snake eyes) and a 12 get 1 in 36 each. Level 21's rule did the work: count the equally likely outcomes, then divide. The skill is making sure the things you count really are equally likely.

title: Chances That Multiply
objective: After this level you can work out the chance of two independent things both happening, like rolling two sixes, by multiplying.
summary: For independent events, the chance of both is the product of their chances: two sixes is 1/6 × 1/6 = 1/36. Draw cards without putting them back and the draws are no longer independent.

cards.headline: What's the chance of rolling two sixes at once?
cards.body: You could list all 36 throws again and hunt for double 6. Or you could use a shortcut that works for any two unconnected chances, from dice to coins to cards. It takes one multiplication.

cards.headline: A fraction of a fraction
cards.body: The first die shows 6 one time in 6. Of those times, the second die also shows 6 just one time in 6. So double 6 happens a sixth of a sixth of the time: 1/6 × 1/6 = 1/36. That matches Level 22's grid, where double 6 was exactly 1 of the 36 throws. The rule: when two events are independent, the chance of both is their chances multiplied.

cards.headline: It keeps multiplying
cards.body: The rule stretches to as many independent events as you like. Two heads in a row: 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4. Three in a row: 1/8. Each extra flip halves the chance again, so ten heads in a row happens about once in 1,024 tries. Multiplying chances that are less than 1 always gives something smaller, which is why long runs are rare before they start.

cards.fact: Multiply only when one result leaves the other alone.
cards.context: Draw a card from a 52-card deck, put it back and shuffle: the second draw starts fresh, so the draws are independent. A heart, then another heart, is 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16. Keep the first heart out, though, and the deck has changed: only 12 hearts are left among 51 cards. Without replacement, the first pick changes the chances for the second.

title: The Chance of At Least One
objective: After this level you can work out the chance of "at least one" by first finding the chance of none, as with a six in four rolls.
summary: An event and its opposite add up to 1, so "at least one" is 1 minus "none". No six in four rolls is 625/1,296 (about 48%), so at least one six is about 52%, as de Méré suspected.

cards.headline: A gambler in Pascal's day wondered about betting on a six in four rolls.
cards.body: The Chevalier de Méré, a French gambler, suspected it was a better bet than a similar one with two dice. Checking by listing every way four rolls can land would take all night. There's a far quicker route: work out the chance of the thing not happening.

cards.headline: Chance it happens = 1 minus chance it doesn't
cards.body: An event and its opposite cover everything that can happen, so their chances add up to 1. If a six has a chance of 1/6, no six has a chance of 5/6. That flip is the key to "at least one" questions. At least one six hides many cases: one six, two, three or four. No six at all is a single case, and Level 23's multiplying handles it.

cards.headline: De Méré's bet, solved
cards.body: No six on one roll: 5/6. No six in four independent rolls: 5/6 × 5/6 × 5/6 × 5/6, which is 625 out of 1,296, about 48%. So at least one six comes up about 52% of the time. A small edge, but a real one. De Méré asked Pascal, whom you met in Level 1, whether this bet really beat a two-dice version, and Pascal proved his hunch right.

title: Coins Have No Memory
objective: After this level you can explain what makes events independent and why a coin that landed heads five times is still 50/50.
summary: Independent events have no memory: after five heads, a fair coin is still 50/50. Six heads in a row is rare before you start (1 in 64), but so is every other sequence of six flips.

cards.headline: Heads, heads, heads, heads, heads. Is tails due?
cards.body: Almost everyone feels it is. Five heads in a row seems to call for a correction. Yet the coin about to be flipped is the same coin, with the same two faces, that you started with.

cards.headline: Independent means the past doesn't count
cards.body: Two events are independent if knowing that one happened doesn't change the chance of the other. Coin flips are the classic case: a coin is a disc of metal with nothing inside keeping score. So after five heads, the sixth flip is still 1 in 2 for heads. Dice work the same way: your first roll doesn't change the chances for your second.

cards.headline: Rare before, ordinary after
cards.body: Before you start, six heads in a row is rare: Level 23's multiplying gives 1 in 64. But once five heads have landed, that rarity is spent. The only thing left to decide is the sixth flip, and it's 50/50. In fact HHHHHH and HHHHHT are equally likely before you begin, and so is every other particular run of six flips: each is 1 in 64.

mascot.line: Keep this: a streak is only rare before it happens. Once it's here, the next flip knows nothing about it.

cards.fact: Decks remember. Coins don't.
cards.context: Level 23's cards had real memory: keep hearts out of a deck and fewer hearts are left to draw. A coin has no deck to run down. So the law of averages does not say that after a run of heads, a head becomes less likely. Every flip starts from scratch.

title: The Gambler's Fallacy
objective: After this level you can explain the gambler's fallacy using the 1913 Monte Carlo roulette run where black came up 26 times.
summary: The gambler's fallacy is believing that after a streak, a different outcome is due. At Monte Carlo in 1913, black came up 26 times in a row and gamblers lost millions betting on red.

cards.headline: 18 August 1913, Monte Carlo: black, black, black... 26 times.
cards.body: At one roulette table, the ball kept landing on black. As the streak grew, so did the crowd, and so did its bets on red. Surely red was due.

cards.headline: The mistake has a name
cards.body: The gambler's fallacy is the belief that after a long streak of one outcome, a different outcome has become more likely. It feels like fairness: the wheel owes you some red. But a roulette wheel is like Level 25's coin. Each spin is independent, so the chance of red on spin 27 was exactly what it was on spin 1.

cards.headline: How the crowd lost
cards.body: The bettors moved their money to red, spin after spin, feeling that red was due, and black kept coming. By the end of the 26 blacks, they had lost millions. Their error was treating a streak's rarity as a force. The run was astonishing before it began, but once it had happened, it said nothing about the next spin.

cards.fact: The law of averages doesn't push back.
cards.context: The law of averages does not say that after lots of black, red becomes more likely. The wheel keeps no score, just like a coin. Level 28 shows what really happens over thousands of spins: an early streak isn't paid back. It simply gets drowned out.

title: Streaks and Clumps
objective: After this level you can explain why truly random sequences contain more streaks and clusters than people expect.
summary: Randomness is streaky: 200 real tosses typically hold a run of about eight, while fakes rarely pass five. Basketball's hot hand, once called an illusion, is still debated.

cards.headline: A teacher can spot fake coin tosses just by their streaks.
cards.body: Half a class tosses a real coin 200 times. The other half makes up 200 tosses. With one simple check, the teacher sorts most of them correctly. The giveaway? The fakes are too tidy.

cards.headline: Real randomness is streaky
cards.body: In 200 real tosses, the longest run of all heads or all tails is typically about eight. Students inventing tosses rarely write a run longer than five, because long runs don't feel random. Statistician Mark Schilling ran this test in his classes and sorted real from fake about 85% of the time. Real chance clumps; people smooth it out.

cards.headline: Why streaks turn up anyway
cards.body: Level 23 showed that any one long run is rare before it starts. But 200 flips give a run many places to start, so somewhere a run of several heads in a row is almost bound to appear. A streak on its own isn't a sign that something is off. It's what randomness looks like.

cards.fact: Is the hot hand real? Still argued.
cards.context: Basketball fans believe a player who has just made shots is more likely to make the next. A famous 1985 study by Gilovich, Vallone and Tversky called that an illusion. In 2018, economists Joshua Miller and Adam Sanjurjo showed the study had counted streaks in a subtly biased way; correcting it reversed the conclusion. Whether fans overrate the hot hand is still open.

title: The Law of Large Numbers
objective: After this level you can explain why results settle close to the true chance over many tries but swing wildly over a few.
summary: Over a few tries, shares swing widely; over many, they settle near the true chance. Kerrich got 5,067 heads in 10,000 tosses. Early luck is not paid back, just swamped by later tries.

cards.headline: During World War II, a prisoner tossed a coin 10,000 times.
cards.body: John Kerrich, an English mathematician, was held in a prison camp in Denmark during the war. He used the time to test one of probability's big promises, by hand, one toss at a time.

cards.headline: Few tries swing, many tries settle
cards.body: Toss a fair coin 10 times and there's only about a 66% chance of getting 40% to 60% heads (4 to 6 heads). With 100 tosses, the chance of landing between 40% and 60% rises to 96%. With 1,000, it's almost 100%. That's the law of large numbers: as tries pile up, the share of heads gets closer and closer to the true chance.

cards.headline: Kerrich's 10,000 tosses
cards.body: Kerrich's count: 5,067 heads out of 10,000 tosses, a share of about 50.7%. Close to half, just as the law promises. The Swiss mathematician Jakob Bernoulli gave the first proof of the law, published in 1713. Kerrich showed it at work on a real coin.

mascot.line: Keep this: the share settles, but the count doesn't have to. That's why luck doesn't even out in the short run.

cards.fact: Luck isn't paid back. It's swamped.
cards.context: Kerrich ended 67 heads over an even 5,000. The law never promised the count would come out even: the gap between heads and half the tosses doesn't shrink to zero. What shrinks is that gap compared with the number of tosses. So early luck isn't cancelled by later tails. It's swamped: 3 heads in the first 10 tosses barely matters after 1,000.

title: The Birthday Problem
objective: After this level you can explain why 23 people are enough for a better than even chance that two share a birthday.
summary: In a group of 23 people, the chance two share a birthday is 50.7%. The trick is counting pairs (253 of them) and working out the chance that nobody matches.

cards.headline: 23 people in a room. Better than even odds that two share a birthday.
cards.body: It sounds far too few. There are 365 days to choose from, after all. Yet with just 23 people, a shared birthday is more likely than not. The secret is in what you're counting.

cards.headline: Count pairs, not people
cards.body: The usual mistake is thinking about your own birthday. The question is whether any two people match, and 23 people make 253 different pairs: the first person pairs with 22 others, the next with 21 more, and so on down to 1. Each pair is a fresh chance for a match. With 253 chances, a match stops sounding strange.

cards.headline: Level 24's trick does the math
cards.body: It's easier to find the chance that nobody matches. The second person misses the first one's birthday 364 times in 365. The third must miss both: 363 in 365. Keep multiplying, one person at a time. By the 23rd person, the chance of no match has sunk just below half, so the chance of at least one match is 50.7%.

cards.fact: At 57 people, a match is about 99% certain.
cards.context: The chance climbs fast because pairs grow much faster than people: 23 people make 253 pairs, but 57 people make 1,596. The math assumes birthdays are spread evenly over 365 days and leaves out leap years. Real births aren't perfectly even, but the difference this makes is negligible.

title: Odds and Probability
objective: After this level you can turn odds like "3 to 1 against" into a probability and back again.
summary: Odds compare the chances against with the chances for; probability compares the chances for with the whole. Add the two numbers of the odds to find the whole: 3 to 1 against is 1 in 4.

cards.headline: Pick a card. The odds it's a heart are "3 to 1 against". What's the chance?
cards.body: Not 3 in 4, and not 1 in 3. Odds and probability are two ways of saying the same chance, and they're easy to mix up. By the end of this level you'll switch between them in your head.

cards.headline: Odds compare two piles. Probability uses the whole deck.
cards.body: A standard deck has 52 cards in four suits of 13. Draw one: 13 cards are hearts and 39 aren't. Odds compare the chances against with the chances for: 39 to 13, which shrinks to 3 to 1 against. Probability compares the hearts with the whole deck: 13 out of 52, or 1 in 4. Same draw, same chance, two different ways of saying it.

cards.headline: Odds to probability: add the two numbers
cards.body: To turn odds into a chance, add both numbers to find the whole. "3 to 1 against" means 3 ways to lose and 1 way to win, 4 in all. So the chance of winning is 1 in 4, or 25%. It's Chapter 1's question again: out of what? For odds, the whole is hiding in plain sight. You just have to add it up.

mascot.line: People mix these up all the time. "To" compares wins with losses. "In" compares wins with everything.

cards.fact: Going back, split the whole into wins and losses.
cards.context: A 1 in 5 chance means 1 win to 4 losses: 4 to 1 against. Likely events flip around. An 80% chance is 80 wins to 20 losses, which shrinks to 4 to 1 in favor. And a 50% chance is 1 to 1, a true toss-up.

title: Expected Value
objective: After this level you can work out the average result of a bet over many plays by weighing each outcome by its chance.
summary: A bet's expected value is its average result per play over many plays: multiply each outcome by its chance and add. It is an average, not a promise about any single play.

cards.headline: Heads, you win $3. Tails, you lose $2. Should you play?
cards.body: It feels close. One number settles it: the expected value, the average a bet pays per play if you play it over and over.

cards.headline: Weigh each outcome by its chance, then add
cards.body: Heads and tails each come up half the time, so weigh each result by one half. Winning $3 counts as $1.50. Losing $2 counts as minus $1. Add them: $1.50 minus $1 is 50 cents. That's the expected value of one flip. The recipe works for any bet: multiply each outcome by its probability, then add the results.

cards.headline: An average, not a promise
cards.body: You'll never win exactly 50 cents on a flip. You win $3 or lose $2. Expected value is an average over many plays: play 100 times and you'd expect to finish about $50 ahead, though any real run of flips wanders around that. That's why it's called expected, not guaranteed.

cards.fact: A $2 game with a 1 in 100,000 chance at $100,000 is worth about minus $1 a play.
cards.context: This one comes from a statistics textbook. The prize weighed by its chance is $100,000 ÷ 100,000, or $1 per play. You pay $2. So on average you lose about $1 every time you play. A negative expected value means a game takes back more than it gives. Keep an eye out: the next few levels are full of them.

title: Why the Casino Always Wins
objective: After this level you can explain the house edge, using the extra green pockets on an American roulette wheel.
summary: An American roulette wheel has 38 pockets but pays single numbers 35 to 1, as if it had 36. The gap is a house edge of about 5.26% (2.7% on a single-zero wheel).

cards.headline: An American roulette wheel has 38 pockets. It pays as if it had 36.
cards.body: That small gap is the whole business. Here's how two green pockets turn a game of luck into a steady income for the casino.

cards.headline: Two green pockets
cards.body: The wheel has 38 pockets: 1 to 36 in red and black, plus a green 0 and 00. Bet $1 on one number and a win pays 35 to 1: you collect $35 and keep your dollar. But with 1 winning pocket and 37 losing ones, the true odds are 37 to 1 against. A 35 to 1 payout would be fair only on a wheel of 36 pockets.

cards.headline: Where the casino's cut comes from
cards.body: Picture betting $1 on one number for 38 spins, with your number hitting once, just as the average says. You staked $38 and get back $36: $35 in winnings plus your dollar. You're $2 down. That's 2 parts in 38, or about 5.26%: the house edge. In Level 32's terms, the bet's expected value is minus 5.26 cents per dollar.

cards.fact: Almost every bet on the American wheel carries the same edge: about 5.26%.
cards.context: Red or black, odd or even, a single number: the payouts are set as if the green pockets weren't there. A European wheel has just one green 0, which cuts the edge to about 2.7%. Any one player can get lucky tonight. But expected value is the long-run average, so across many bets the casino keeps close to 5.26 cents of every dollar.

title: Is Insurance a Bad Bet?
objective: After this level you can explain why insurance loses money on average for buyers yet can still be a sensible choice.
summary: Insurance premiums must cover claims, running costs and profit, so buyers lose a little on average. Risk-averse people pay that extra to swap a big possible loss for a small sure cost.

cards.headline: Insurance companies make money. So, on average, their customers lose it.
cards.body: As a bet, insurance loses. Yet buying it can still be a smart move. Expected value is part of the story, but not all of it.

cards.headline: A pool that pays out less than it takes in
cards.body: Insurance is a pool. Members pay a regular premium, and anyone who suffers a covered loss is paid from the pool. Over time, the premiums have to cover three things: the claims, the cost of running the company, and its profit. So the average customer pays in more than they get back. For the buyer, insurance has a negative expected value.

cards.headline: The $1,000 bike
cards.body: Say your bike is worth $1,000, and each year there's a 1 in 100 chance you'll have to replace it. Your expected loss is $1,000 × 1/100, or $10 a year. An insurer would charge that $10 plus a little extra, and the extra is how it makes money. Most years you pay and get nothing back. That's the deal working, not failing.

cards.fact: You pay a little extra to swap a big gamble for a small, sure cost.
cards.context: Economists call people risk-averse when they'll pay more than a gamble's expected loss to avoid it, and most people are. Insurance exists so that no single event hits you too hard. So the question isn't only "is the average in my favor?" It's also "what happens to me if the bad outcome comes?"

summary: When a host who knows where the car is opens a goat door, switching wins 2 times in 3: your first pick was a goat 2 times in 3, and then the other closed door hides the car.

cards.headline: Three doors: one car, two goats. The host opens a goat door. Do you switch?
cards.body: It's tempting to shrug: two doors left, so why bother? In 1990 the columnist Marilyn vos Savant told Parade magazine readers to switch. Thousands of letters poured in, many from academics, insisting she was wrong. She wasn't.

cards.headline: The rule that makes the puzzle
cards.body: The puzzle is named after Monty Hall, host of the TV game show Let's Make a Deal. You pick a door. Then the host, who knows where the car is, opens one of the other two doors and shows a goat. He never opens your door, and he never reveals the car. His knowledge is the whole puzzle: the door he opens isn't random.

mascot.line: Two doors left does not mean 50-50. The host's knowledge tipped the scales before you chose.

cards.headline: Count the three ways it can start
cards.body: Your first pick is the car 1 time in 3. Then switching loses. But 2 times in 3, your first pick is a goat. The host must open the other goat, so the only other closed door hides the car, and switching wins. Switch every time and you win 2 games in 3. Stay every time and you win 1 in 3.

cards.fact: Switching wins 2 times in 3: odds of 2 to 1 in your favor.
cards.context: Another way to see it: your first door had a 1 in 3 chance, and the other two doors together had 2 in 3. When the host opens the goat among those two, that whole 2 in 3 rests on the one door he left shut. Switching is like trading your one door for both of the others.

title: Should You Risk the Parking Ticket?
objective: After this level you can use expected value to compare two everyday choices, like paying for parking or risking a fine.
summary: Compare a sure cost with the expected cost of a gamble. With a $4 meter, a $50 fine and a 1 in 5 chance of a ticket, skipping costs $10 on average. The choices break even at a chance of 8 in 100.

cards.headline: The meter costs $4. The fine is $50. Pay, or take your chances?
cards.body: Nobody calls it a bet, but it is one. Let's put made-up round numbers on it and let expected value decide.

cards.headline: The cost of skipping, on average
cards.body: Suppose 1 time in 5 you'd get a ticket. Skipping then costs $50 × 1/5, or $10 on average, against a sure $4 at the meter. Paying saves you $6 a visit on average. Even if tickets came only 1 time in 10, skipping would cost $5 on average: still more than the meter.

cards.headline: Find the break-even point
cards.body: Where would the choice flip? When the expected fine equals the meter: the chance times $50 equals $4. That happens at a chance of 4 in 50, or 8 in 100. Unless tickets were rarer than that, the meter is the better deal. Finding the break-even chance works for any either-or choice: it tells you how likely the bad outcome must be before the gamble stops paying.

cards.fact: Expected value counts only what you put into it.
cards.context: The sum above includes the fine and nothing else. Any cost you leave out of the calculation, like lost time or a ruined afternoon, can't show up in the answer. So a neat average can make a gamble look cheaper than it feels. Level 35's risk-averse buyer knew that already.

title: Same Average, Different Risk
objective: After this level you can explain why two choices with the same expected value can differ in how badly things might go.
summary: Two bets can share an expected value and still be very different: a sure $50 and a coin flip for $100 or nothing both average $50. Expected value hides the spread, so also ask how bad it can get.

cards.headline: A: $50 for sure. B: flip a coin for $100 or nothing. Which do you take?
cards.body: Level 32's number calls them equal: both have an expected value of $50. Most people still grab the sure thing. They aren't bad at math.

mascot.line: Keep this: expected value gives you the middle, not the edges. Always ask how bad it can get.

cards.headline: The average hides the spread
cards.body: Both choices average $50, but look at what can actually happen. A pays exactly $50 every time. B pays $100 or $0, and never $50. Expected value squeezes all the outcomes into one average, so it can't show how far apart they are. Two bets can share an average and still be very different bets.

cards.headline: Same average, bigger stakes
cards.body: Now two coin bets. In one, you win or lose $1. In the other, you win or lose $1,000. Both have an expected value of $0, since the win and the loss cancel out. But only the second can cost you $1,000 on one bad flip. When the worst case is something you couldn't afford, the spread matters more than the average.

cards.fact: Risk-averse people prefer a sure thing to a gamble with the same expected value.
cards.context: That's a preference about risk, not an arithmetic error. It's why insurance sells (Level 35), and why a fair-looking bet can still be a poor idea. So judge any gamble on two things: its average, and how bad it can get.

title: Let the Computer Roll the Dice
objective: After this level you can explain how running thousands of pretend trials on a computer estimates a chance too hard to calculate.
summary: A Monte Carlo simulation estimates a chance by running many random pretend trials and counting the successes. Stanislaw Ulam had the idea over solitaire in 1946; it first ran on ENIAC in 1948.

cards.headline: In 1946, a mathematician recovering from illness got stuck on solitaire.
cards.body: Stanislaw Ulam wanted the chance that a hand of 52 cards would come out. Working it out exactly was monstrously hard. His way around the math now runs on computers everywhere.

cards.headline: Don't calculate. Deal.
cards.body: Ulam's idea: instead of doing the math, lay the cards out a hundred times and count how many games come out. Successes divided by tries estimates the chance. Each game has to start from a fresh random shuffle, and the more tries you run, the closer the share tends to get to the true chance. That's a Monte Carlo simulation: lots of pretend trials, then count.

cards.headline: Named after a casino
cards.body: Ulam talked it over with John von Neumann, and they saw it could crack hard problems in their work at Los Alamos, like tracing the paths of neutrons. A colleague, Nick Metropolis, named it Monte Carlo, after the casino town Ulam's uncle kept borrowing money to visit. The first runs were on the ENIAC computer in 1948.

cards.fact: A simulation convinced Paul Erdős about Monty Hall.
cards.context: The great mathematician reportedly doubted Level 36's answer until computer simulations confirmed it. You could do the same: play 3,000 pretend games, always switching, and you'd expect to win about 2,000. Today the same trick measures risks in science, finance, transport, health and manufacturing.

cards.body: Chapter 4 handed you the tools one level at a time. This checkpoint lines them up into three questions you can ask of any bet.

Multiply each outcome by its chance and add: that's the expected value. Third: how bad can it get? title: Absolute Risk: The Real Numbers
objective: After this level you can state a risk as an absolute number, like 2 in 1,000, and explain why that is the number that matters to you.
summary: Absolute risk is the plain chance that something happens: how many, out of how many, over how long. It is the number that is about you; "twice as likely" is not.

cards.headline: "Raises your risk!" Of what, out of how many, and by when?
cards.body: Health news loves the word risk. But a risk you can use is a plain number: how many people something happens to, out of how many, over what stretch of time. That plain number has a name: absolute risk.

cards.headline: Absolute risk: the plain chance
cards.body: Absolute risk is the chance that something happens to a person in a group over a set time. Picture a shuffled deck of 52 cards. Your absolute risk of drawing a heart is 1 in 4, or 25%. Your risk of drawing the queen of diamonds is 1 in 52, just under 2%. No comparisons and no spin: just how often it happens.

cards.headline: Three parts: how many, out of how many, by when
cards.body: A complete risk has three parts. "2 in 1,000 over 10 years" says how many (2), out of how many (1,000) and over how long (10 years). Leave out the time and the number goes vague: the chance of something happening over one year is different from the chance over a lifetime. As a percent, 2 in 1,000 is 0.2%.
cards.callout: A risk = how many, out of how many, over how long

mascot.line: Keep this: a risk isn't a real number until you know out of how many, and over how long.

cards.fact: Absolute risk is the number that is about you.
cards.context: It says how likely the thing is for someone like you over that time. A comparison such as "twice as likely" can't tell you that on its own; it needs the absolute risk underneath. And as Level 7 showed, a count of people like 2 in 1,000 is easier to picture than 0.2%.

title: Relative Risk: "Doubles Your Risk!"
objective: After this level you can explain why "doubles your risk" can mean going from 1 in 10,000 to 2 in 10,000, and ask for the absolute numbers.
summary: Relative risk compares groups ("doubles", "triples") but hides how likely the thing is. From a tiny start, even tripling adds few cases, so always ask for the absolute risks.

cards.headline: "Doubles your risk!" Doubles it from what?
cards.body: Going from 1 in 10,000 to 2 in 10,000 is doubling. So is going from 1 in 10 to 2 in 10. Same headline, wildly different news. This level shows you how to tell them apart.

cards.headline: Relative risk: a comparison, not a chance
cards.body: Relative risk compares two groups: the risk in one against the risk in the other. A relative risk of 1 means no difference; 2 means twice as likely. That is useful for spotting what matters. But it tells you how many times, not how many people. On its own, a relative risk says nothing about how likely the thing is at all.

cards.headline: "Triple the risk" in a real headline
cards.body: In 2012, a study of more than 175,000 young people found that repeated CT scans in childhood could triple the risk of leukemia and brain tumors. Scary. Now the absolute numbers: about one extra case of each for every 10,000 head scans in children aged 10 or under, over the next 10 years. The researchers stressed that when a child needs a scan, its benefits should outweigh that small risk.

cards.fact: Tiny start, big multiplier, small change.
cards.context: When a risk starts very small, even tripling it adds few cases. When it starts big, a modest rise can hit many people: doubling 1 in 10 means 1,000 extra cases per 10,000 people. So when you hear "doubles" or "triples", ask for the two absolute risks, before and after.

title: How Many Must Take the Pill?
objective: After this level you can explain the number needed to treat: how many people take a treatment for one of them to benefit.
summary: The number needed to treat turns an absolute risk drop into people: halving a 2% risk means about 100 people take a pill for one to benefit. The ideal NNT is 1.

cards.headline: A pill halves heart attacks. How many must take it to help one person?
cards.body: Take a guess before you read on. Two? Ten? In the example this level walks through, the answer is 100. Both numbers are true, and the gap between them is the whole lesson.

cards.headline: Half of a small number is a small number
cards.body: Picture a study in which the 2-year risk of a heart attack is 2% on a dummy pill (a placebo) and 1% on the real one. That is a 50% relative reduction: the headline number. But the absolute drop is just 1 percentage point, one person in 100. So 100 people would need the pill for 2 years to prevent one heart attack.

cards.headline: Meet the number needed to treat
cards.body: That 100 has a name: the number needed to treat, or NNT. It is how many people must take a treatment over a set time for one of them to benefit. It first appeared in the medical literature in 1988. To find it, divide 100 by the drop in absolute risk in percentage points. A drop from 10% to 5% is 5 points, and 100 ÷ 5 = 20.

cards.fact: The perfect treatment has an NNT of 1.
cards.context: If a treatment helps everyone, you treat 1 person to help 1. If it helps half, 2; a quarter, 4. Think of free throws: a 25% shooter needs about 4 tries per basket. Back in the heart-attack example, of 100 people who take the pill, about 98 would have been fine anyway, about 1 has a heart attack regardless, and about 1 is spared.

title: Is Flying Safer Than Driving?
objective: After this level you can explain why a risk comparison depends on what you count per: per trip, per mile or per hour.
summary: Per mile, flying is far safer than driving; per trip, the gap closes, because crashes cluster at takeoff and landing. A risk comparison depends on what it is counted per.

cards.headline: Is flying safer than driving? First ask: safer per what?
cards.body: You can count travel deaths per mile, per hour or per trip. Each is a fair rate, and each can crown a different winner. So the honest answer to the question starts with a question of its own.

cards.headline: Per mile, flying wins by a landslide
cards.body: Divide deaths by the miles people travel, and the gap is enormous. In 2023 US figures, people in cars and trucks died at more than 100 times the rate for people traveling by air, mile for mile. That is the fair rate for comparing two ways of covering the same distance.

cards.headline: Per trip, the race gets close
cards.body: Most fatal airliner accidents happen around takeoff and landing, not in the long cruise between: of those from 2004 to 2013, only about 1 in 10 happened in cruise. So a flight carries much of its risk however far it goes. Count deaths per journey instead of per mile, and analyses of 1990s data found flying riskier than a car trip. Same crashes, new divider.

cards.fact: The "per" you pick decides the winner.
cards.context: A risk comparison is a comparison of rates, and a rate means little until you know what it is counted per. Per mile, per hour and per trip each answer a different question, and each can rank the ways of traveling differently. That is Level 10's question in a new place.

title: Base Rates: Start With How Common
objective: After this level you can explain why you should start with how common something is before judging a single case.
summary: The base rate is how common something is in the whole population. Start there before judging one case: when you hear hoofbeats, think horses, not zebras.

cards.headline: You hear hoofbeats outside. Horse or zebra?
cards.body: Unless you live next to a zoo, you guess horse. Doctors have a saying built on exactly that hunch, and it holds one of the most useful ideas in this chapter.

cards.headline: Think horses, not zebras
cards.body: "When you hear hoofbeats, think horses, not zebras." The saying is usually credited to Theodore Woodward of the University of Maryland School of Medicine, who reportedly used a version of it from the 1940s. It reminds doctors that a common explanation is far likelier than a rare one. "Zebra" even became medical slang for a surprising, rare diagnosis.

cards.headline: The base rate: how common, before any clue
cards.body: The share of people in a whole population who have something is its prevalence, or base rate. It can be given as a percent, or per 10,000 or 100,000 people. It is where you start: before you judge any one case, ask how common the thing is to begin with.

cards.fact: A clue that fits both explanations can't beat a big base-rate gap.
cards.context: Picture a made-up town of 10,000 people. This week 1,000 have a cold and 1 has a rare illness, and both cause a cough. Among people coughing, colds outnumber the rare illness 1,000 to 1. That is why test results and other clues are read against how common a condition is. Horses first.

title: Two Ways a Test Can Be Right
objective: After this level you can explain a test's sensitivity (catching true cases) and specificity (clearing healthy people) in plain words.
summary: Sensitivity is how many people with a condition a test catches; specificity is how many without it the test clears. Moving the cutoff trades one against the other.

cards.headline: A smoke alarm can fail in two ways.
cards.body: It can stay silent during a real fire, or shriek at burned toast. Medical tests can go wrong in the same two ways, and each has its own number. Learn both and you'll read any test result more wisely.

cards.headline: Four ways a test result can land
cards.body: Cross what the test says (positive or negative) with the truth (has it or doesn't) and you get four boxes. True positive: sick, and flagged. True negative: healthy, and cleared. False negative: sick but missed, the silent alarm. False positive: healthy but flagged, the burned toast.

mascot.line: People mix these two up. Sensitivity is about the people who have it; specificity is about the people who don't.

cards.headline: Sensitivity catches, specificity clears
cards.body: Sensitivity is about people who have the condition: a test with 90% sensitivity catches 90 of every 100 of them and misses 10. Specificity is about people who don't: a test with 90% specificity correctly clears 90 of every 100 healthy people and gives the other 10 a false alarm.

cards.fact: You usually can't max out both.
cards.context: Many tests give a reading, and someone picks the cutoff for calling it positive. Lower the cutoff and you catch more true cases, but more healthy people get flagged too: sensitivity rises, specificity falls. A touchier smoke alarm misses fewer fires and ruins more toast.

title: Why Most Positives Can Be False
objective: After this level you can show with a count of 10,000 people why a good test for a rare condition can give mostly false alarms.
summary: Count 10,000 people: with 1% sick and a 90%/90% test, 90 true positives meet 990 false alarms, so only 1 in 12 positives is real. The base rate decides.

cards.headline: A test that is right 9 times in 10 says yes. The chance it's real: 1 in 12.
cards.body: No trick and no faulty test. Just counting. Take 10,000 imaginary people and follow them through the test, the way Level 7 recommended: counts of people, not percents.

cards.headline: Step 1: start with the base rate
cards.body: Say 1% of them have a condition: 100 people out of 10,000. The other 9,900 don't. The test has 90% sensitivity, so it catches 90 of the 100 and misses 10. So far, so good.

cards.headline: Step 2: count the false alarms
cards.body: The test also has 90% specificity, so it clears 90% of the 9,900 healthy people: 8,910 of them. The other 10% get a false alarm. That is 990 people told they might have something they don't. Notice the mismatch: 990 false alarms against 90 true catches.

cards.context: Healthy people vastly outnumber sick ones, so even a small share of them swamps the true cases. title: Changing Your Mind by the Right Amount
objective: After this level you can explain Bayes' idea in words: start from the base rate and let each new piece of evidence shift it.
summary: Bayes' idea in words: start from the base rate and let each piece of evidence move it. A second positive lifts 1 in 12 to 45%; a negative cuts 1 in 100 to about 1 in 900.

cards.headline: Your positive result means a 1 in 12 chance. Then a second test says yes too.
cards.body: Should you panic now? Shrug? Neither. There is a right amount to change your mind, and an 18th-century English minister worked out the idea behind it.

cards.headline: Bayes: start with the base rate, then update
cards.body: Thomas Bayes was an English minister who died in 1761. His friend Richard Price found an essay on probability among his papers and sent it to the Royal Society, which published it. Its big idea, in words: begin with a starting chance, such as a base rate, then let each new piece of evidence shift it. The updated chance becomes the start for the next clue.

mascot.line: This connects: Level 45's base rate is where Bayes starts, and Level 47's count is Bayes in action.

cards.headline: Two positives: from 1 in 12 to nearly half
cards.body: Back to Level 47's 1,080 positives: 90 sick, 990 healthy. Give them a second test of the same quality whose mistakes are unrelated to the first. It catches 81 of the 90 sick and flags 99 of the 990 healthy. Now 81 of 180 positives are real: 45%. That is why doctors often follow a positive screening test with a second, more specific one.

cards.fact: Evidence can push the chance down, too.
cards.context: Suppose instead the first test is negative. Of the 8,920 people who test negative, only 10 are sick. Your chance falls from 1 in 100 to about 1 in 900. Changing your mind by the right amount means neither ignoring evidence nor leaping to certainty: start from the base rate, then let each result move you.

title: The Prosecutor's Fallacy
objective: After this level you can explain why a tiny chance of the evidence happening by accident is not the chance of innocence, using the Sally Clark case.
summary: In the Sally Clark case, a 1 in 73 million figure wrongly assumed independent deaths and was misread as the chance of innocence: the prosecutor's fallacy. Her convictions were quashed in 2003.

cards.headline: A jury once heard the number 1 in 73 million.
cards.body: It sounded like proof. It wasn't, for two reasons this chapter has trained you to spot. This is a true story about a family's tragedy, so we'll stick to what the record shows.

cards.headline: The case
cards.body: Sally Clark, an English solicitor, was convicted in November 1999 of murdering her two baby sons. At her trial, a medical expert witness told the jury that the chance of two cot deaths (sudden infant death syndrome) in a family like hers was 1 in 73 million. He got it by squaring the chance of a single cot death.

cards.headline: Mistake 1: treating the deaths as unconnected
cards.body: Squaring a chance only works if the two events are independent, like two coin tosses. But unknown genetic or environmental factors may make a second cot death in the same family much more likely. In October 2001 the Royal Statistical Society said the 1 in 73 million figure had no statistical basis.

cards.headline: Mistake 2: the prosecutor's fallacy
cards.body: Some press reports called 1 in 73 million the chance that the deaths were accidental. That is the prosecutor's fallacy: mixing up how unlikely the evidence is under one explanation with how likely that explanation is. Cot death and murder were both very unlikely explanations, yet the deaths had happened. The fair question is how likely the deaths are under each one, side by side.

cards.fact: In January 2003, the Court of Appeal quashed her convictions.
cards.context: The Criminal Cases Review Commission found that the medical and statistical evidence at her trial had been misleading, and that important bacteriological evidence had not been disclosed. The lesson for anyone weighing evidence: a tiny chance of the evidence arising by accident is not the chance of innocence.

title: Tasting the Soup: Why We Sample
objective: After this level you can explain how a small sample can describe a whole population, the way one spoonful tells you about a pot of soup.
summary: A sample is a portion of a population, studied because checking everyone is costly. Its statistic estimates the population's parameter, as a stirred spoonful tells you about the pot.

cards.headline: You don't drink the whole pot to know if the soup needs salt.
cards.body: One spoonful does it. Pollsters do the same with a whole country: opinion polls often ask 1,000 to 2,000 people and speak for everyone. This chapter is about when a spoonful is enough, and when it lies.

cards.headline: The pot and the spoonful
cards.body: The whole group you want to know about is the population: every voter in a country, every student in a school. The part you actually examine is the sample. Why not just check everyone? Examining a whole population takes a lot of time and money, and often it's simply impossible. So you study a portion and learn about the rest from it.

cards.headline: From the spoon's number to the pot's
cards.body: Any number you work out from the sample, like an average or a percentage, is a statistic. The matching number for the whole population, the one you really want, is the parameter. The statistic is your estimate of it. How good is that estimate? It depends above all on one thing: how well the sample represents the population.
cards.callout: Statistic: from the sample. Parameter: the whole population.

mascot.line: Keep this for the whole chapter: a sample is only as good as the stirring.

cards.fact: Stir first, then taste.
cards.context: A 1946 pamphlet on opinion polls put it plainly: a cook stirs the broth thoroughly, then dips out one spoonful to test the whole kettle. The stirring is what lets one spoonful speak for the pot. Then probability, Level 1's second job, tells you how confident you can be in what you tasted.

title: Random Means Everyone Gets a Chance
objective: After this level you can explain why a fair sample gives every member of the population the same chance of being picked.
summary: A fair sample gives every member the same chance of being picked. Handy samples tilt, and even a lottery fails if the capsules aren't mixed, as the 1969 US draft lottery showed.

cards.headline: In 1969, a lottery set the order of the US draft. December lost.
cards.body: Every birthday was supposed to have the same chance. Yet men born in December drew early numbers far more often than a fair draw would give. The problem wasn't the idea of a lottery. It was a badly stirred box.

cards.headline: The rule: everyone gets the same chance
cards.body: A fair sample follows one rule: every member of the population starts with the same chance of being picked. That's random sampling. Pollsters take it literally. Gallup has a computer generate phone numbers at random, so an unlisted number is as likely to ring as a listed one. Chosen this way, every adult has an equal chance of landing in the sample.

cards.headline: Grab whoever's handy, and the sample tilts
cards.body: Break the rule and you get sampling bias: some people are less likely to be chosen, and the results can mislead. A textbook example: a radio station with 20,000 listeners wants to know if they'd like more music or more talk. It asks the first 200 people at one of its music concerts, and 176 want more music. No surprise. It asked people who came out for music.

cards.headline: The draft lottery's lumpy box
cards.body: In December 1969, 366 capsules, one for each day of the year, were drawn one at a time to set the order of the US draft. But the capsules had gone into the box month by month, January through December, and the mixing afterward wasn't enough to undo that. December birthdays drew disproportionately low numbers, meaning earlier calls. Statisticians charged that the lottery was not random.
cards.callout: Random isn't a label. It's a process you have to carry out.
