title: The Poll That Picked the Wrong Winner
objective: After this level you can explain how the 1936 Literary Digest poll got 2 million answers and still called the election wrong.
summary: In 1936 the Literary Digest got 2.4 million ballots back and still picked the loser. Its lists leaned well-off and its replies were biased; size can't fix bias.

cards.headline: About 2.4 million answers. The wrong winner.
cards.body: In 1936 the Literary Digest magazine mailed about 10 million straw ballots, got about 2.4 million back, and called the US presidential election. It picked the loser. You may have met this story in How Government Works; here's the statistics of why it failed.

cards.headline: The giant poll against the small one
cards.body: The Digest predicted Alf Landon would beat President Franklin Roosevelt with about 57% of the vote. Roosevelt won in a landslide, with more than 60%. Meanwhile George Gallup, using a far smaller sample chosen systematically and scientifically, said Roosevelt would win handily. The small poll beat the giant one.

cards.headline: Who was on the list?
cards.body: The Digest drew names from lists such as telephone owners and car registrations. In the middle of the Great Depression, those lists leaned toward better-off Americans. A sample can only pick people who are on the list it's drawn from. Leave people off, and they never get a chance.

mascot.line: People mix these up all the time: size fixes luck, not bias. A huge sample can still be a lopsided one.

cards.fact: A bigger sample shrinks chance error. It doesn't shrink bias.
cards.context: A 1988 study found two problems working together: the Digest's sample was biased, and so were the replies. Had everyone it polled answered, it would at least have picked Roosevelt to win. More answers from a tilted sample just give you the same wrong answer, more confidently.

title: Why 1,000 People Are Enough
objective: After this level you can explain why a random sample of about 1,000 can describe a whole country, whatever its size.
summary: The sample a poll needs depends on the precision wanted, not the population's size. About 1,000 random people give about plus or minus 3 points; more buys little.

cards.headline: Your chance of being in a Pew poll is about 1 in 26,000.
cards.body: Pew's panel has about 10,000 adults, out of about 260 million in the US. Yet its polls speak for all of them. How can so few speak for so many? The answer surprises almost everyone: the size of the country barely matters.

cards.headline: The size of the pot doesn't matter
cards.body: Taste a well-stirred small pot and a well-stirred giant vat: one spoonful tells you about as much in each. Samples work the same way. The sample size you need depends on how precise you want to be, not on how big the population is. The same 1,000 people can represent a population of 100,000 or of 1,000,000.

cards.headline: Bigger helps, then barely
cards.body: Size still matters, just not how you'd guess. The margin of error falls steeply as a sample grows from 100 to 1,000 people. After that it crawls: a random sample of about 1,000 gives about plus or minus 3 points, and doubling from 1,000 to 2,000 cuts it by only about one point. That's why national polls usually ask 1,000 to 2,000 people.

cards.fact: The mix matters more than the size.
cards.context: Remember Level 53: about 2.4 million answers from tilted lists lost to Gallup's far smaller, carefully drawn sample. Randomness buys fairness. Only then does size buy precision, and after about 1,000 people it buys less and less.

title: What "Plus or Minus 3" Means
objective: After this level you can explain what a poll's margin of error covers and why a lead smaller than it is too close to call.
summary: Plus or minus 3 at 95% confidence means about 95 of 100 repeats land within 3 points of the truth. The margin on a lead is about double, and it counts only sampling error.

cards.headline: "48%, plus or minus 3." So is it 48 or not?
cards.body: Every serious poll carries that little tail. It isn't small print to skip. It says how far the poll's number could honestly be from the truth, and when a headline lead is really a tie.

cards.headline: What the 3 covers
cards.body: Plus or minus 3 at the usual 95% confidence means this: run the same survey 100 times, and about 95 results land within 3 points of the true value. So 48% really says somewhere from 45% to 51%. About 5 times in 100, the truth sits outside even that range. And notice the unit: percentage points, not percent. That's Level 5 at work.

mascot.line: Common mix-up: a lead bigger than 3 points isn't enough. Check it against about double the margin.

cards.headline: A lead needs about double
cards.body: Here's the catch in a two-way race. If one candidate's share is too high by chance, the other's is likely too low, so the margin on the gap between them is about double. With plus or minus 3 each, a 5-point lead could really be anywhere from -1 to +11. It takes a lead of about 6 points to be confident it isn't luck.

cards.fact: The margin only counts the luck of the draw.
cards.context: It measures sampling error: the wobble from asking some people instead of everyone. Loaded wording and people who won't answer aren't in it. And it grows for small groups inside a poll: about 160 people get about plus or minus 8 points.

title: The People Who Don't Answer
objective: After this level you can explain nonresponse bias: why the people who skip a survey can skew its results.
summary: Phone response rates fell from 36% to 6%. Low response alone isn't fatal; bias comes when answering is tied to the topic, as with volunteering, and as with the 1936 Digest.

cards.headline: In 1997, 36% of the people Pew phoned took part. By 2018, 6%.
cards.body: Pew Research Center's typical phone poll now hears from only a small slice of the people it tries. The ones who pick up are a special crowd. Does that ruin polls? Surprisingly, not always.

cards.headline: Who picks up?
cards.body: Pew's typical phone survey response rate fell from 36% in 1997 to 9% in 2012 and 6% in 2018. Robocalls may be part of it: a poll call looks like one more unknown number, and phones flag some as spam. The danger isn't the low number itself. It's nonresponse bias: if the people who skip a survey differ from those who answer on what it measures, the results skew.

cards.headline: The volunteers who answer everything
cards.body: Pew studies in 1997, 2003, 2012 and 2016 found little link between response rates and accuracy. What matters is whether the topic is tied to who answers. Politics mostly wasn't. Volunteering was: in 2012, 55% of Pew's respondents said they'd volunteered in the past year, against 27% in the government's Current Population Survey. The urge to help out seems to include helping pollsters.

cards.context: Remember Level 53. The Digest's replies were biased too: a 1988 study found that had everyone it polled answered, it would at least have picked Roosevelt to win. Nonresponse, not just the list, helped sink it.

title: Weighting: Fixing a Lopsided Sample
objective: After this level you can explain how pollsters weight answers so a sample's mix of ages and backgrounds matches the population.
summary: Pollsters weight answers so a sample's mix of age, sex, race, education and region matches Census figures. Weighting fixes the mix, not traits it doesn't measure, and widens the margin.

cards.headline: Your poll has too few young adults. Now what?
cards.body: No sample comes out a perfect miniature of the country, because some people are simply easier to reach. So pollsters do the next best thing: they make some answers count more than others.

cards.headline: Easy to reach, overcounted
cards.body: Left alone, polls overrepresent people who are easier to reach and underrepresent those who are harder to interview. So after the answers come in, pollsters weight them. Gallup, for example, gives each respondent a weight so the sample's mix of gender, race, age, education and region matches the Census Bureau's latest estimates.

cards.headline: Counting some voices double
cards.body: Say young adults are 20% of the population but only 10% of your sample. Each young adult's answers then count about twice, and overrepresented groups count a little less, until the mix matches. Doing this for several traits, one after another until they all line up, is called raking. It's the standard method at Pew and many other pollsters.

mascot.line: If you remember one thing: weighting can balance who answered, not why they answered.

cards.fact: Weighting fixes the mix, not the mindset.
cards.context: It can only balance the traits a pollster weights on. Remember Level 56's volunteers: standard weighting falls short when polls measure volunteering, so those estimates stay too high. And weighting has a price: it makes the margin of error bigger.

title: The Wording Changes the Answer
objective: After this level you can spot how the wording and order of survey questions can shift the answers people give.
summary: Same question, different words, different answers: in 1941, 75% would 'not allow' speeches against democracy but only 54% would 'forbid' them. Answer lists and order matter too.

cards.headline: Forbid, or not allow? To you, the same. To a poll, not at all.
cards.body: Logically, refusing to allow something and forbidding it are the same answer. In 1941 a pollster asked Americans a question both ways and got very different results. Words aren't neutral wrapping. They're part of the question.

cards.headline: Same question, different words
cards.body: The test was a split-ballot experiment: a random half of the sample got one wording and the other half the other, so any gap comes from the words. Of those who answered, 75% said the US should "not allow" public speeches against democracy. Only 54% said it should "forbid" them. One leading explanation: forbid sounds harsher, so fewer people will say it.

cards.headline: The menu and its order
cards.body: The answer list matters too. When Pew offered the economy as a choice for the issue that mattered most to voters, 58% picked it; asked with no list, only 35% named it. Order counts as well: on the phone people lean toward the options they hear last, and on a screen toward those at the top. So careful pollsters shuffle the order for each person.

cards.fact: Agree-or-disagree questions tilt toward agree.
cards.context: Some people tend to agree with whatever statement they're read, so better practice offers a choice between two statements. And because words shift answers, comparing polls over time needs the exact same wording. None of this is in the margin of error, which counts only sampling error.

title: Click Polls and Online Reviews
objective: After this level you can explain why polls where people choose to take part measure who cares most, not what most people think.
summary: When people choose whether to take part, a poll measures who cares most. Opt-in polls have no margin of error, and online ratings form a J because extreme opinions post.

cards.headline: "Vote now!" Thousands click. What have you learned?
cards.body: Mostly, who felt like clicking. When people choose for themselves whether to take part, a poll stops measuring what most people think. It starts measuring who cares most.

cards.headline: Picking yourself
cards.body: In a self-selected, or opt-in, poll, people choose themselves: a website button, a call-in line. Nobody knows each person's chance of being included, so the results may not represent anyone but the people who joined. That's why Pew won't base its polls on volunteers: they'd likely be more politically interested and engaged than the average American.

cards.headline: Why ratings look like a J
cards.body: Online reviews are opt-in polls too. Product ratings often pile up at 5 stars, with a smaller heap at 1 star and few in between: a J shape. Buyers with extreme opinions are likelier to write a review to "brag or moan" than those who thought it was fine. When researchers had everyone rate the same product, the ratings formed a single hump instead.

cards.fact: No random sample, no margin of error.
cards.context: A margin of error applies only when everyone had a known chance of being picked. Opt-in polls don't qualify, however many clicks pile up. So ask Level 10's question: out of what? For a click poll, the honest answer is out of the people who chose to answer.

title: Watching vs. Testing
objective: After this level you can tell an observational study, which watches what people already do, from an experiment, which changes something.
summary: An observational study watches what people already do; an experiment changes something and compares. Watching shows links, but other habits can explain them.

cards.headline: People who take vitamin E are healthier. So vitamin E works, right?
cards.body: It's a classic statistics textbook puzzle. Vitamin E takers really do show better health on average. Whether the pill causes it depends on how the data were gathered, and that's the big question of this chapter.

cards.headline: Watching: the observational study
cards.body: One way to learn is to watch. In an observational study, researchers record what people already do, such as taking vitamin E, without changing who does it. The catch: vitamin E takers often do other healthy things too. They exercise, eat well, take other supplements and don't smoke. Any of those could explain their better health. Watching shows a link, but it can't say which habit made the difference.

cards.headline: Testing: the experiment
cards.body: The other way is to change something yourself. In an experiment, researchers introduce an intervention, like giving one group vitamin E and another group none, and then measure what happens. The design goal: the only difference between the groups is the planned treatment. Then, if the groups end up different, the treatment is the prime suspect.
cards.callout: Observational: watch. Experiment: change something, then compare.

cards.fact: Sometimes watching is the only fair option.
cards.context: Researchers can't ethically expose people to something harmful just to see what happens. So some questions can only be answered by watching. Those results stay open to dispute, because the groups may differ in hidden ways that explain the link. The next few levels show how a good experiment shuts that door.

title: The Control Group
objective: After this level you can explain why an experiment needs a comparison group, using James Lind's 1747 scurvy trial.
summary: In 1747 James Lind gave six remedies to six pairs of similar scurvy patients on one diet. The citrus pair recovered, and the other pairs were the comparison that proved it.

cards.headline: In 1747, a ship's surgeon ran one of history's famous fair tests.
cards.body: Sailors on HMS Salisbury had scurvy, and there were several treatments in use. James Lind didn't just pick his favorite. Starting on 20 May 1747, he tried six of them side by side on 12 sick sailors.

cards.headline: First, make the patients alike
cards.body: Lind chose 12 sailors whose cases were, in his words, "as similar as I could have them". They lay together in the same quarters and ate one diet common to all. Then two men got each of six remedies: cider, elixir of vitriol, vinegar, sea water, two oranges and a lemon, or a medicinal paste. With everything else the same, any difference in recovery would point to the remedy.

cards.headline: Every pair was a yardstick
cards.body: The pair eating oranges and lemons did best. One was fit for duty after six days; the other recovered well enough to nurse the rest of the sick. Notice how we know it worked: not because two men got better, but because they got better than the other ten. Historians credit Lind for taking care to compare like with like.

mascot.line: This is Level 10's habit in a new place: a share needs an "out of what", and a result needs a "compared with what".

cards.fact: A result means little until you ask: compared with what?
cards.context: Modern trials build that comparison in on purpose. A control group gets no treatment or an inactive placebo, and its results are set beside the treated group's. Changes can happen by chance, so only the gap between the groups can be linked to the treatment.

title: Why Flip a Coin to Pick Groups
objective: After this level you can explain how random assignment balances hidden differences between groups, which is why it makes a fair test.
summary: Random assignment lets chance pick the groups, so hidden differences spread evenly and only the treatment differs. The 1948 streptomycin trial used sealed random numbers.

cards.headline: Lind never said how he chose which sailor got which remedy.
cards.body: Suppose he'd handed the oranges to the two strongest men. Their recovery would prove nothing. How you pick the groups can settle the result before the test even starts.

cards.headline: Let chance do the picking
cards.body: When researchers choose who gets a treatment, the groups can end up different in ways that bias the comparison, even with the best intentions. Random assignment takes the choice away. A coin, a die or a list of random numbers decides. A fair coin lands heads with probability 0.5, so every volunteer has a 50% chance of either group, whoever they are.
cards.callout: Random assignment: chance, not people, picks the groups.

cards.headline: It balances what nobody measured
cards.body: Here's the clever part. People differ in countless ways: fitness, diet, how sick they are. With random assignment, those hidden differences get spread evenly among the groups, so the only difference left is the one the researchers imposed. You don't even need to know what the hidden differences are. Chance balances them anyway.

cards.fact: In 1948, sealed envelopes kept doctors from choosing.
cards.context: Britain's Medical Research Council was testing the antibiotic streptomycin on patients with tuberculosis of the lungs. Patients were allocated using random numbers, and the list was kept in sealed envelopes, unknown to the investigators, so no doctor could steer anyone into either group. It is often called the first randomized controlled trial in medicine.

title: Placebos and Blinding
objective: After this level you can explain why trials use placebos and keep people blind to who got what.
summary: A placebo is an inactive look-alike, so the gap between drug and placebo groups is the drug's own effect. Blinding keeps expectations from tipping the results.

cards.headline: Expecting to feel better can make you feel better.
cards.body: Doctors call it the placebo effect: a real benefit that comes from a person's expectation that a treatment will help. That's lovely for patients and a headache for anyone testing a new drug. How can you tell what the drug did from what the hoping did?

cards.headline: The placebo: a pill that does nothing on purpose
cards.body: A placebo is an inactive substance that looks like the treatment being tested. In a placebo-controlled trial, volunteers are randomly split: one group gets the real treatment, the other gets the placebo. Both groups get the expectation; only one gets the drug. So the gap between the groups' results is the drug's own effect, over and above hope.

cards.headline: Blinding: nobody knows who got what
cards.body: A placebo only works as a control if people can't tell which pill they got. So in a blinded study, participants aren't told who is getting the active treatment and who the placebo. In a double-blind study, the researchers working with them don't know either, so their hopes can't tip how patients are treated or how results are judged.
cards.callout: Double-blind: neither patients nor researchers know who got the real thing.

cards.fact: When patients can't be blinded, the judges still can.
cards.context: Some treatments are impossible to disguise. In one textbook study, people solved mazes wearing a flower-scented mask for some and an unscented one for others. They could smell the difference, so they couldn't be blinded. But the researchers timing the mazes could be kept in the dark about which mask was which.

title: Comparing Like With Like
objective: After this level you can explain how a hidden third factor can distort a comparison and how studies adjust for it by comparing similar groups.
summary: A confounder is a hidden third factor that differs between groups and affects the result. Comparing like with like, as in age-adjusted rates, removes its effect.

cards.headline: Meditators get less heart disease. Is it the meditating?
cards.body: Imagine a study that follows people for years and finds exactly that. Before you buy a cushion, ask what else meditators might have in common.

cards.headline: The hidden third factor
cards.body: People who meditate may also exercise more and eat healthier diets. Either could protect the heart. When the groups you compare also differ in something else that affects the outcome, the comparison is confounded, and that something is a confounder (statisticians also say lurking variable). It makes one thing look like the cause when another is doing the work.

cards.headline: Compare like with like
cards.body: When you can't run an experiment, you can still make the comparison fairer by comparing similar people. Age is the classic case: it's a prime factor in mortality, so places with more older residents almost always have much higher overall death rates. Health statisticians work out a rate for each age group, then combine them using the same standard mix of ages for every place. That's an age-adjusted rate.

cards.fact: Level 6 fixed size. Age adjustment fixes age.
cards.context: A rate per person stops a big city looking worse just for having more people. An age-adjusted rate goes one step further: it stops an older county looking worse just for having older people. Each fix removes one unfair difference, and what's left is a closer comparison of like with like.

title: How Strong Is a Link?
objective: After this level you can read a scatter plot and explain what a correlation near 0, near 1 or below 0 says about how closely two things move together.
summary: A scatter plot shows two measurements as dots; the correlation, from -1 to +1, rates how tightly they follow a straight line. The sign is direction, the size is strength.

cards.headline: Hotter days, more ice cream. But how tightly do the two move together?
cards.body: In a textbook example, a shop owner writes down the noon temperature and the cones sold on nine days. Plot them and a pattern jumps out. Statistics can put a single number on how strong it is.

cards.headline: One dot per day
cards.body: Put temperature along the bottom and cones sold up the side, and each day becomes one dot. That's a scatter plot. When the dots drift upward from left to right, as they do here, hotter days tend to bring more cones: a positive link. If they drifted downward, one would tend to fall as the other rose: a negative link.

cards.headline: The correlation: a score from -1 to +1
cards.body: The correlation coefficient, written r, rates how closely the dots follow a straight line. It always lands between -1 and +1. Near +1 means a tight upward line; near -1, a tight downward one; near 0, no straight-line pattern at all. Exactly 1 or -1 would put every dot on a line, which real data almost never do. The sign gives the direction; the size gives the strength.

mascot.line: People mix these up: -0.8 is a stronger link than +0.5. The minus sign only says the line slopes down.

cards.fact: Always look at the dots, not just the number.
cards.context: A correlation only measures straight-line patterns. Dots that curve, rising and then falling, can score 0 even though the two things are clearly related. And even a strong correlation doesn't show that one thing causes the other.

title: What "Statistically Significant" Means
objective: After this level you can explain honestly what a significant result and a p-value tell you: how surprising the data would be if nothing were going on.
summary: Fisher's tea test shows the idea of significance: how surprising would this be by luck? A p-value measures that; it is not the chance a finding is true.

cards.headline: A lady said she could taste whether the milk went in first.
cards.body: In his 1935 book The Design of Experiments, the statistician Ronald Fisher turned that claim into a famous test. The question it answers: when is a result too good to be luck?

cards.headline: What would luck look like?
cards.body: Fisher's plan: 8 cups, 4 with milk first and 4 with tea first, served in random order. She had to pick out the 4 milk-first cups. There are 70 ways to choose 4 cups from 8, so someone just guessing would get them all right only 1 time in 70, about 1.4%. Sort all 8 correctly, and pure luck becomes a hard story to believe.

cards.headline: That's what a p-value measures
cards.body: A p-value asks the same question of any study: if nothing were going on, how surprising would results at least this striking be? A small p-value means luck alone would rarely produce them. Fisher wrote that it was usual and convenient to draw the line at 5 percent. Results that clear the line are called statistically significant.
cards.callout: Small p-value: this would be rare if nothing were going on.

mascot.line: Common mix-up: a p-value starts by assuming nothing is going on, so it can't also be the chance that something is.

cards.fact: A p-value is not the chance the finding is true.
cards.context: That's the classic misreading, and the American Statistical Association warned against it in 2016. A p-value doesn't measure the chance the hypothesis is true, or that the data came from luck alone. So p = 0.05 isn't a 5% chance the result is a fluke. It only says how badly the data fit the idea that nothing is going on.

title: Significant Isn't the Same as Big
objective: After this level you can explain why a result can be statistically significant yet too small to matter, and why effect size counts.
summary: Statistical significance doesn't measure how big or important an effect is. Huge samples make tiny effects significant, so ask for the effect size.

cards.headline: "Significant" sounds like "important". In statistics, it isn't.
cards.body: A statistically significant result is one that would be surprising if nothing were going on, as Level 67 showed. The label doesn't measure how big the effect is, or whether anyone should care.

cards.headline: Surprising isn't the same as large
cards.body: The American Statistical Association put it plainly in its 2016 statement: a p-value, or statistical significance, does not measure the size of an effect or the importance of a result. A tiny, dull effect can clear the significance bar. So can a huge one. The word "significant" can't tell you which you're looking at.

cards.headline: Big samples make tiny effects significant
cards.body: How does a tiny effect clear the bar? Sheer numbers. With a large enough sample, a test will almost always find a significant difference unless the effect is exactly zero. In a study of 10,000 people, even a negligible difference between groups is likely to come out significant. Sometimes "significant" mostly means the study was huge.
cards.callout: Enough people, and almost any difference turns significant.

mascot.line: Keep this: significant answers "surprising?" The effect size answers "how much?" You need both.

cards.fact: So always ask: how big is the effect?
cards.context: The effect size is how big the difference between groups actually is: how many more people recovered, or how many points scores rose. Experts call it the main finding of a study. Unlike significance, it doesn't grow just because more people took part.

title: Do It Again: Replication
objective: After this level you can explain why one study is rarely enough and what happened when scientists tried to repeat published results.
summary: Luck can pass a 5% test, so one study is a clue, not proof. When 100 psychology studies were repeated in 2015, 36% of repeats were significant against 97% of originals.

cards.headline: Scientists redid 100 published studies. Most weren't significant again.
cards.body: It happened in 2015, and every one of the originals had been published in a psychology journal. So why would a repeat fail? The answer starts with what a single significant result can and can't tell you.

cards.headline: Luck passes the test sometimes
cards.body: Level 67's 5% line has a built-in catch. If nothing at all is going on, a test will still come out significant about 5 times in 100 by chance alone. Fisher saw it coming in 1935: no single experiment, however significant, can prove a natural phenomenon. What counts is knowing how to run an experiment that will rarely fail to give a significant result.

cards.headline: The big repeat
cards.body: In 2015, a large team called the Open Science Collaboration put published findings to that test. They repeated 100 experimental and correlational studies from three psychology journals. Of the originals, 97% had statistically significant results. Of the repeats, 36% did. And on average, the repeat effects were half the size of the original ones.

cards.fact: One study is a clue. A repeat is how you check it.
cards.context: Replication is how science sorts sturdy results from lucky ones. In the 2015 project, whether a result came back was better predicted by how strong the original evidence was than by who ran the original or repeat studies. Strong evidence tended to hold up; weak evidence tended to fade.

title: Checkpoint: Experiments and Evidence
objective: After this level you can judge how strong a study's evidence is from its design: control group, randomization, blinding and size.
summary: Evidence has a ladder: observational studies, then randomized controlled trials, then systematic reviews. Judge a study by its control group, randomization, blinding and effect size.

cards.headline: Two studies make the same claim. Which one would you trust?
cards.body: One watched what people already did. The other split volunteers by chance, gave half a placebo and kept everyone blind. This chapter gave you the tools to rank them.

cards.headline: A ladder of evidence
cards.body: Researchers rank evidence roughly like a ladder. Near the bottom sit observational designs, cohort and case-control studies. Above them is the randomized, placebo-controlled trial, often called the gold standard. At the top are systematic reviews, which search out and weigh the studies already done on a question. Lind did an early one: besides his trial, he gathered and judged earlier reports on scurvy.

Then read the numbers honestly
cards.body: Two last checks. Significant means the result would be surprising if nothing were going on, not that it's big: ask for the effect size. And a single study is a clue, not a verdict, so look for a repeat.

title: Reading Any Chart
objective: After this level you can read a chart by checking its title, axes, units and source before looking at its shape.
summary: Read the words before the shape: the title gives the message, the subtitle what, where and when, the axis titles the units, and the source line where the numbers came from.

cards.headline: A line on a chart shoots up. Before you gasp, read the small print.
cards.body: Your eyes go straight to the shape: up, down, flat. But a shape can't tell you what rose, where, when or in what units. The words around the chart can, so they come first.

cards.headline: Title, then subtitle
cards.body: UK government guidance on charts asks for two titles. The main title states the chart's message. The subtitle says what was measured, where and over what time period. Its own example reads: "Number of people living in one person households, England, 1991 to 2021." What, where, when. The title is the chart maker's claim; the subtitle tells you what that claim is about.

cards.headline: Axes: what is counted, and in what units
cards.body: Next, the axes. Each axis title should give its unit of measurement, and every axis should be clearly labelled. That one line of text changes everything. The same rising line means something very different in people or in percent, in totals or in cases per 100,000 people. A chart that hides its units hasn't earned your trust yet.

mascot.line: Keep this: read the words before the shape. Every trick in this chapter hides in something people skipped.

cards.fact: Last check: where did the numbers come from?
cards.context: Guidance says every chart should name the specific source of its data, so you can find it yourself, not just a vague nod to an organization. Title, subtitle, axis units, source: four quick reads before you judge the shape. The rest of this chapter shows what goes wrong when people skip them.

title: The Chopped-Off Axis
objective: After this level you can spot a bar chart whose axis doesn't start at zero and explain how it makes small gaps look huge.
summary: Huff's 1954 gee-whiz graph chopped off an axis to make a 10% rise look big. Bars are judged by length, so a bar chart's axis should start at zero.

cards.headline: In 1954, a book showed how to make a 10% rise look huge. The tool: scissors.
cards.body: Darrell Huff's How to Lie with Statistics didn't just warn about the trick. It gave it a name. Once you know it, you'll start spotting it.

cards.headline: The gee-whiz graph
cards.body: Huff drew a graph of national income rising 10% in a year, with a zero line at the bottom. It looked like a modest climb. Then he chopped off the bottom of the chart. Same numbers, same line, but now it climbed halfway up the page. Nothing was falsified except the impression. He called it the gee-whiz graph, after what it makes you say.

cards.headline: Bars are judged by their length
cards.body: Bars are even easier to fool with. Your eye compares their lengths, so official guidance says a bar chart's axis should start at zero. Try it: two bars show 50 and 52. That's a gap of just 4%, since 2 ÷ 50 = 0.04. Start the axis at 48 instead, and the bars are drawn 2 and 4 units tall. The second now looks twice as big.

cards.fact: A chopped bar axis can turn a 4% gap into a doubling.
cards.context: Line charts get a little more room: guidance allows their axis to start above zero when the values sit in a narrow range, as long as the break is made obvious. For bars, the rule is simple. Look at the bottom of the axis. If it isn't zero, stretch the bars back down in your head before you compare them.

title: Picking the Start Date
objective: After this level you can explain how choosing where a chart starts and ends can make the same trend look like a rise or a fall.
summary: Whoever picks where a chart starts and ends picks its story: a price from 100 to 150 to 120 is up 20% from the start and down 20% from the peak.

cards.headline: "Prices up 20%!" "Prices down 20%!" Same chart, and both are true.
cards.body: It sounds impossible. It isn't. The trick is where each headline chose to start the clock.

cards.headline: Whoever picks the window picks the story
cards.body: A chart of anything over time has to begin and end somewhere, and those dates are a choice. The Royal Statistical Society warns about exactly this: cherry-picking points in time. That can mean starting at an unusual moment, or showing a window too short for the real pattern to appear.

cards.headline: One price, two stories
cards.body: Say a price starts at 100, climbs to a peak of 150, then settles at 120. Start the chart at the beginning: 120 is 20 above 100, and 20 ÷ 100 = 0.2, a 20% rise. Start it at the peak: 120 is 30 below 150, and 30 ÷ 150 = 0.2, a 20% fall. Nothing was made up. Only the starting line moved.

cards.fact: When a chart starts at a convenient moment, ask for the longer view.
cards.context: Guidance from the UK's statistics regulator adds that quoting only the latest figure can mislead if it isn't typical of the wider trend. So check the dates on the axis, and ask what the chart would look like zoomed out. The honest version usually shows the whole ride.

title: Maps That Show Where People Live
objective: After this level you can explain why many maps of totals simply show where people live, and why per person maps tell more.
summary: Shade places by totals and you mostly redraw where people live, as a 2012 xkcd comic joked. Dividing by population turns a map of people into a map of the thing itself.

cards.headline: Three maps of very different things. They look almost exactly alike. Why?
cards.body: In a 2012 comic, xkcd showed a presenter comparing three US maps, each of a different group of people. The maps matched almost perfectly. The joke was that none of them really showed its group at all.

cards.headline: Most maps of totals are maps of people
cards.body: Shade each place by how many people do something, and the darkest patches land on the big cities. Of course they do: that's where the people are. So a map of totals mostly redraws where people live, whatever its title says. That's why the comic's three maps matched. Each was basically a population map.

mascot.line: It connects: this is Level 6's rate per person, painted onto a map.

cards.headline: Divide by the people
cards.body: Mapmakers fix this by normalizing: divide each area's count by its population and map a rate instead, such as cases per 100,000 people. A Penn State mapping course calls the problem population dependence. Skip that division and you get endless maps that just light up population centers. Do it, and big and small places are measured on the same footing.

cards.fact: Before you read a map, read its legend.
cards.context: If the legend counts totals, the map is mostly telling you where people live. If it says per person or per 100,000 people, it's comparing like with like, and a dark patch finally means something.

title: Pies, Pictures and 3D Tricks
objective: After this level you can spot pie charts that don't add to 100% and pictures that exaggerate by growing in two directions at once.
summary: A pie is one whole, so its slices must total 100%. 3D tilts inflate near slices, and Huff's moneybag drawn twice as tall covers four times the area.

cards.headline: A pie chart whose slices add up to more than 100% isn't a pie. It's a warning.
cards.body: Pie charts, picture charts and shiny 3D graphics look friendly. Each has its own way of making some numbers look bigger than they are.

cards.headline: A pie is one whole
cards.body: A pie chart's circle stands for the whole: 100%. So its slices have to add up to 100%. A common way to break that rule is a survey where people could pick more than one answer, like favorite pizza toppings. Those answers can total well over 100%, so they don't belong in a pie. And tilting a pie into 3D makes the slices nearest you look bigger than they are.

cards.headline: Twice as tall, four times as big
cards.body: Picture charts have their own trap, and Huff caught it in 1954. To show a wage of $60 against $30, draw one moneybag twice as tall as the other. Fair? But it's also twice as wide, so it covers four times the area. Read as a solid bag, it looks like eight times the money: $240 instead of $60.

cards.fact: Compare heights, not areas.
cards.context: The Royal Statistical Society warns that icon charts can mislead because comparing areas is harder than comparing heights. When a chart uses pictures, ask how many times bigger the number is, not how many times bigger the picture looks.

title: Two Axes, One Story
objective: After this level you can explain how a chart with two different vertical scales can make any two lines seem to move together.
summary: A chart with a scale on each side lets its maker stretch and shift each line freely, so the lines can cross or chase anywhere. UK guidance says use two charts.

cards.headline: Give two lines two different scales, and they can tell almost any story.
cards.body: Crossing, chasing or moving in lockstep: on a two-axis chart, much of that is decided by whoever draws it.

cards.headline: Two rulers, one picture
cards.body: A dual-axis chart puts one scale on the left and another on the right, each for its own line. Each scale can be stretched or shifted freely, so where the lines sit, and whether they cross, is a design choice. UK government guidance warns that these charts are easily misread and can be manipulated to show almost any relationship.

cards.headline: The line that climbed above
cards.body: The guidance shows a real case. The UK's employment rate for people aged 16 to 64 stayed above 70% from 2009 to 2022. The unemployment rate stayed under 10%. Yet on a dual-axis chart, the lines crossed, and a reader could come away thinking unemployment was higher than employment from 2009 to 2015. On a single scale, the two lines would sit far apart.

cards.fact: Two measures? Two charts.
cards.context: The guidance's fix is simple: give each measure its own chart and its own axis. When you meet a two-axis chart anyway, read each scale separately and don't read anything into where the lines cross. The crossing is a drawing choice, not a fact about the data.

title: Log Scales
objective: After this level you can read a chart where each step up the axis multiplies instead of adds, and explain when that helps.
summary: On a log scale each step multiplies, so 1 to 10 is as far as 10 to 100, and steady doubling becomes a straight line, as on Moore's 1965 chart.

cards.headline: In 1965, Gordon Moore drew explosive growth as a straight line.
cards.body: He was tracking transistors, the tiny switches on computer chips. The trick was in his axis: each step up it multiplied instead of adding.

cards.headline: Each step multiplies
cards.body: On an ordinary axis, each step up adds the same amount. On a log scale, each step multiplies: 1, 10, 100, 1,000. The gap from 1 to 10 is as wide as the gap from 100,000 to 1,000,000. That lets one chart fit a thousand, a million and a billion at equal steps, since each is 1,000 times the one before.

cards.headline: Straight means steady growth
cards.body: Here's the payoff. On an ordinary chart, something that doubles at a steady pace curves upward ever more steeply. On a log scale, that same growth becomes a straight line. That's what Moore's chart showed: the transistor count has doubled roughly every two years, and on a log axis the points line up.

cards.fact: Log scales are useful, and easy to misread.
cards.context: In a 2020 experiment, about 2,000 Americans saw COVID-19 deaths on either a log chart or an ordinary one. Asked a basic question about it, about 84% of the ordinary-chart group got it right, against about 41% of the log group. So check the axis labels first: if each step multiplies, read it that way.

title: Running Totals Always Go Up
objective: After this level you can explain why a cumulative chart keeps climbing even when things are slowing down.
summary: A cumulative chart adds each new count to a running total, so it never goes down. Falling weekly counts show up as a line that climbs more slowly and bends flatter.

cards.headline: A chart of cases climbs every single week. The outbreak is fading anyway.
cards.body: Both can be true at once. It comes down to one word that's easy to miss in a chart's title: cumulative.

cards.headline: A pile only grows
cards.body: A cumulative chart shows a running total: everything counted so far. Each week's new cases are added to the pile, and nothing is ever taken off. So the line can rise or stay flat, but it can never go down, however good the news.

mascot.line: People mix these up all the time: a rising running total doesn't mean things are getting worse. Look for the bend.

cards.headline: Watch the bend, not the climb
cards.body: Say new cases run 100, 80, 60 and 40 over four weeks. Every week is better than the last. Yet the running total reads 100, 180, 240, 280: still climbing. The good news hides in the shape. As weekly counts fall, the total rises more slowly and the line bends flatter. Only when new cases stop does it go flat.

cards.fact: First, find out what is being added up.
cards.context: The Math Doctors put it simply: a cumulative chart will never go down, so check the axis labels and the chart's description to see whether you're looking at a running total or current numbers. For a running total, the question isn't whether it rises. It's how fast.

title: Error Bars and Storm Cones
objective: After this level you can read error bars and a hurricane forecast cone as ranges of uncertainty, not as sizes.
summary: Error bars and hurricane cones draw uncertainty, not size. NHC's cone holds two-thirds of past track errors, so the storm's center strays outside about one time in three.

cards.headline: A hurricane cone looks like a picture of the storm. It isn't.
cards.body: Neither are the little whiskers on a bar chart. Both draw uncertainty: a range where the truth probably lies. Read them as sizes and you'll get the wrong idea.

cards.headline: Whiskers mean "somewhere in here"
cards.body: An estimate is rarely one exact number. The Royal Statistical Society suggests saying "between 190 and 210" rather than just "200", and drawing that range as error bars or shaded areas. The bar shows the estimate; the whiskers show how far off it might be. Different kinds of error bars mean different things, so a good chart says which kind it uses.

cards.headline: The cone is a track, not a storm
cards.body: The National Hurricane Center's cone shows where the storm's center will probably go. Its width comes from the forecasters' own track record: it's sized so two-thirds of past forecast errors fall inside. So about one time in three, the center strays outside the cone. It widens further ahead, where past forecasts missed by more.

cards.fact: The storm is bigger than its cone.
cards.context: A hurricane isn't a point. NHC notes that its effects can reach hundreds of miles from the center, well beyond the cone. Sitting just outside the cone doesn't mean you're out of danger. It means the center probably won't pass over you.

title: Simpson's Paradox
objective: After this level you can explain how a trend in every group can reverse when the groups are combined, using the 1973 Berkeley admissions data.
summary: Berkeley admitted 44% of men and 35% of women in 1973, yet women did better in four of the six biggest departments. A trend in every group can reverse when the groups are combined.

cards.headline: In 1973, Berkeley seemed to favor men. Department by department, it didn't.
cards.body: The overall numbers looked damning. Then researchers looked one department at a time, and the pattern turned around. Same applicants, same decisions, opposite story. How can both be true?

cards.headline: The overall numbers
cards.body: In fall 1973, Berkeley's graduate programs admitted about 44% of the 8,442 men who applied, but only about 35% of the 4,321 women. That's a gap of 9 percentage points. Level 2 showed that percents put groups of different sizes on one scale, so this looks like a fair comparison. Hold that thought.

cards.headline: Inside the departments
cards.body: Split the numbers by department and they flip. In Department A, one of the six biggest, 82% of the 108 women who applied got in, against 62% of the 825 men. In four of those six departments, women were admitted at a higher rate. The difference was where people applied: women more often chose departments that were hard to get into, men the easier ones.

cards.fact: A trend in every group can reverse when the groups are combined.
cards.context: That's Simpson's paradox. Berkeley's overall percents mixed departments with very different odds, so they partly measured who applied where. In a 1975 paper in Science, three researchers found a small bias in favor of women once departments were taken into account. Before trusting a combined percent, ask what it lumps together.

title: Regression to the Mean
objective: After this level you can explain why an extreme result is usually followed by a more ordinary one, with no cause needed.
summary: A score is part skill, part luck, and luck is redrawn, so extremes drift back toward average. Galton saw it in 1886 in family heights. It runs both ways, so no cause is needed.

cards.headline: Your best game ever is usually followed by a worse one. That's not a slump.
cards.body: No curse, no pressure, no lost magic. An extreme result tends to be followed by a more ordinary one, simply because of how results are made. Statisticians call it regression to the mean.

cards.headline: Skill plus luck
cards.body: Any score mixes two things: what you can really do, and luck. On a quiz, the luck is which questions happen to come up. The top scorer usually had both, real knowledge and a kind set of questions. Next quiz, the knowledge stays but the luck is redrawn, so their score will probably come down toward the average. A player's best-ever game works the same way.

cards.headline: Galton's tall families
cards.body: Francis Galton spotted the pattern in 1886, comparing hundreds of adult children with their parents. Very tall parents tended to have children taller than average but less tall than themselves; very short parents had children closer to average too. Stranger still, it runs backward: tall children have parents who are, on average, less tall than they are. Children can't shape their parents, so no cause is needed.

mascot.line: If you remember one thing: an extreme result is partly luck, and luck doesn't repeat on request.

cards.fact: An extreme result is usually followed by a more ordinary one, with no cause needed.
cards.context: It happens anywhere a measurement is repeated: test scores, blood pressure, a team's season. The trap is inventing a story for the fall, like a jinx or praise that went to someone's head. First ask whether the first result was extreme. If it was, some drift back toward average was coming anyway.

title: Why Remedies Seem to Work
objective: After this level you can explain how regression to the mean makes a treatment or a new rule look effective when people start at their worst.
summary: Patients, roads and hospitals picked at their worst drift back toward average anyway, so before-and-after flatters any remedy. A similar untreated group shows the real effect.

cards.headline: The sickest patients often improve fastest after a new treatment. Why?
cards.body: It looks like proof the treatment works. Sometimes it is. But Level 82's drift back toward average was coming anyway, and it can make almost anything look like a cure.

cards.headline: Starting at the worst
cards.body: When a new treatment arrives, some doctors are tempted to try it first on the patients who are most ill. Those patients usually show a sharp, gratifying improvement. Part of the reason is regression to the mean: an extreme reading is partly bad luck, and bad luck rarely repeats. Anyone picked because they're at their worst has lots of room to drift back toward average.

cards.headline: New rules get the same boost
cards.body: A sudden spike in road crashes is often chance, so a crackdown launched after one will seem to cut crashes. Give extra help to the hospitals at the bottom of a league table and most will climb; reward the ones at the top and they'll tend to slip. Statistician Stephen Senn put it bluntly: judged only by before and after, even sacrificing a chicken at a dangerous junction would look effective.

cards.fact: The fix: compare with a similar group that didn't get the treatment.
cards.context: Both groups start at their worst, so both drift back toward average. Only the difference between them shows what the treatment or rule itself did. That's why the best tests randomly split patients, or struggling hospitals, into groups instead of trusting a simple before and after.

title: Small Places, Extreme Numbers
objective: After this level you can explain why the smallest groups show both the highest and the lowest rates, just by chance.
summary: The US counties with the lowest and highest kidney cancer death rates were both small and rural. One case swings a small place's rate, so small groups fill both ends by chance.

cards.headline: Kidney cancer is rarest in tiny rural counties. It's also most common there.
cards.body: Two maps, two tidy stories: clean country living on one, rural hardship on the other. Both stories are wrong. The real reason fits in one word: small.

cards.headline: Two maps that look alike
cards.body: Statistician Howard Wainer showed two maps of US counties, shaded by kidney cancer death rates among men from 1980 to 1989. The counties in the lowest 10% were mostly very rural, in the Midwest, South and West. So were the counties in the highest 10%, many right next door. Whatever story explains one map can't also explain the other.

cards.headline: One death makes a hot spot
cards.body: Remember Level 6: a rate divides a count by the population. In a county of 100 people, no cancer deaths gives a rate of 0, the lowest possible. One death makes it 1,000 per 100,000, among the highest. Big counties can't swing like that. Wainer found the ones with millions of people all sat near 5 per 100,000, while small ones ranged from 0 to 20.

cards.fact: Small groups land at both extremes, by chance alone.
cards.context: The same thing shows up in schools. Among 1,662 Pennsylvania schools with fifth-grade reading scores, the smallest were overrepresented among both the 50 best and the 50 worst. So when the top and bottom of a ranking are both crowded with small places, suspect chance before hunting for a cause.

title: How Filters Create Fake Links
objective: After this level you can explain how studying only a selected group can create a link between two traits that isn't there in everyone.
summary: SAT verbal and math scores rise together, but behind a 1320 admission cutoff the link flips. Filtering on two traits can create a false link, as Berkson saw with hospital patients.

cards.headline: At a picky college, the math stars seem to be weaker readers. Why?
cards.body: Is math crowding out words? No. The pattern among the students is real, but nothing in their heads makes it. It comes from the gate they all had to pass through.

cards.headline: A link made by a gate
cards.body: Allen Downey used real SAT data. Across test-takers, verbal and math scores rise together: strong at one usually means strong at the other. Then he imagined a college that admits only combined scores of 1320 or more. Among its students, the link flips: higher verbal scores go with lower math scores. Same kind of people, just filtered.

cards.headline: Why the gate flips it
cards.body: To get in with a so-so math score, you needed a great verbal score, and the reverse. Students weak at both never made it, so they're missing from the picture. Statisticians who study admissions describe the same pattern: an admitted student with an unusually low test score is more likely to have exceptional reference letters.

mascot.line: This is Chapter 1's question again: out of what? A link found only among the filtered may not hold for everyone.

cards.fact: Filter a group on two traits, and a false link between them can appear.
cards.context: Joseph Berkson spotted this in 1946 with hospital patients. Being admitted depends on having some illness, so studying only patients can make a disease seem linked to a cause when it isn't. Before trusting a link, ask who was let through the gate, and who was left outside it.

title: Test Enough Things, Something Wins
objective: After this level you can explain why testing many ideas at once guarantees some "significant" flukes, and how p-hacking exploits that.
summary: At the usual 5% bar, about 1 test in 20 of nothing passes by luck. A dead salmon 'lit up' until the statistics were corrected. Reporting only the winners is p-hacking.

cards.headline: Scientists found brain activity in a dead salmon. The fish wasn't the problem.
cards.body: The salmon was put in a brain scanner and "shown" photos of people in social situations. The software found spots in its brain that seemed to respond. The lesson wasn't about fish. It was about how many questions were asked at once.

cards.headline: The 1-in-20 bar
cards.body: Results are often called "statistically significant" when they clear a bar, usually 5%. The bar is set so that when nothing real is going on, a test clears it by luck only about 5% of the time. That's Level 7's 1 in 20. For one test, it's a small risk. But run 100 tests where nothing is happening, and you'd expect about 5 flukes to pass anyway.

cards.headline: Thousands of tests in one fish
cards.body: A brain scan checks a huge number of tiny spots, each as its own test: up to 130,000 in one study. With that many chances, some spots pass by luck. In the salmon study, published in 2010, the unadjusted statistics found "active" spots. A correction that raises the bar when you run many tests, such as dividing the 5% by the number of tests, made them vanish. The team won an Ig Nobel Prize in 2012.

cards.fact: Test enough things and something will look significant by chance.
cards.context: Doing that and reporting only the winners has a name: p-hacking. Try many measures, groups or analyses, then show the ones that pass. In 2016 the American Statistical Association warned against it and said sound conclusions need full reporting and transparency, not just the hits.

title: Cancer Clusters and Random Clumps
objective: After this level you can explain why clusters of cases appear by chance and how investigators check whether one is real.
summary: Cancer is common, so cases clump by chance. Investigators compare observed with expected cases; one, rare or unusual cancers are the signs. Few suspected clusters are confirmed.

cards.headline: Several neighbors on one street get cancer. Surely that can't be chance?
cards.body: Worries like this reach local and state health departments, and they check them. But random cases don't spread out evenly across a map. They clump. The job is telling a clump from a cause.

cards.headline: Random means clumpy
cards.body: A cancer cluster is more cancer cases than expected among people in one area over a set period. The catch: cancer is fairly common, so cases can seem to cluster even when nothing connects them. Scatter a handful of rice on a map and some grains land in little piles, for no reason at all.

cards.headline: Observed versus expected
cards.body: So investigators count. They compare the cases observed with the number expected, worked out from cancer rates in a larger population, adjusted for age. They look harder when the cases are one type of cancer, a rare type, or in an age group it doesn't usually strike. And they watch the boundary: drawing the area around the cases after spotting them can create a cluster out of nothing.

cards.fact: Of 567 suspected cancer increases checked, 72 were confirmed and 1 had a clear cause.
cards.context: That comes from a 2012 review of 428 investigations by US health agencies since 1990. Three of the confirmed increases were linked to a possible exposure. A clump is always worth checking, but most are never confirmed as real increases.

title: True for the Group, Not for You
objective: After this level you can explain why a pattern across groups or places may not hold for the individuals in them.
summary: In 1930, states with more immigrants had higher literacy, yet immigrants were less often literate: they lived in states where the native-born read well. Groups aren't individuals.

cards.headline: In 1930, states with more immigrants read better. Did immigrants read better?
cards.body: It's the obvious conclusion, and it's backwards. The pattern across states was real. What it seemed to say about individual people was wrong.

cards.headline: The pattern across states
cards.body: Using the 1930 census, sociologist W. S. Robinson lined up the 48 states. The higher a state's share of residents born abroad, the higher its share who could read and write. Put on a chart, it's a clear trend: more immigrants, more literacy.

cards.headline: Now count people
cards.body: Count people instead of states and it reverses. Of foreign-born residents aged 10 and over, about 10 in 100 could not read and write; among the native-born, about 3 in 100. The explanation: immigrants tended to live in states where the native-born were relatively literate. The states' pattern was real. It just wasn't a fact about individual immigrants.

mascot.line: Common mix-up: a pattern across states is a fact about states. To learn about people, you have to measure people.

cards.fact: A pattern across groups may not hold for the individuals in them.
cards.context: Assuming it does is called the ecological fallacy. Robinson's 1950 paper concluded that links measured across areas can't stand in for links between individuals. So when a headline links two things across countries, states or schools, ask: was anyone actually measured one by one?

title: Nobody Is Average
objective: After this level you can explain why almost no one is average on many measures at once, using the US Air Force's 1950 cockpit study.
summary: Of 4,063 men in the Air Force's 1950 survey, none was average on all 10 of Daniels's measurements. Each step cut the group, so designing for the average fits no one.

cards.headline: The Air Force measured over 4,000 pilots to find the average one. Nobody fit.
cards.body: The survey was meant to help build better-fitting cockpits. A young Air Force scientist, Lt. Gilbert S. Daniels, asked a simple question first: how many pilots actually are average?

cards.headline: A generous average
cards.body: Daniels picked 10 body measurements that matter for design, such as height, chest size and sleeve length. He didn't demand an exact match. Anyone in roughly the middle 30% of the group on a measurement counted as "approximately average" on it. Then he checked all 4,063 men from the 1950 survey against the 10 measurements, one after another.

cards.headline: Watch the crowd shrink
cards.body: Of 4,063 men, 1,055 were of average height. Of those, 302 also had an average chest. Only 143 of them also had average sleeves. Each measurement cut the group again, and after all 10, not one man was left. One pilot might have long arms and short legs, another a big chest and small hips. Everyone is average somewhere; nobody is average everywhere.

cards.fact: Daniels called the "average man" a misleading basis for design.
cards.context: His 1952 report said the idea is especially misleading when more than one measurement matters at once. So when something is built for "the average person", ask how many real people that describes. On enough measures at once, the answer can be nobody.

title: Checkpoint: Statistical Traps
objective: After this level you can explain which trap, from Simpson's paradox to survivorship bias, is at work in a surprising statistic.
summary: Surprising statistics often come from a mix of groups, an extreme that drifts back, small groups or many tests, or a filter or group-level pattern. Survivorship bias is one more filter.

cards.headline: A statistic surprises you. Before you believe it, name the trap.
cards.body: Chapter 9 has shown you how honest numbers can tell the wrong story. This checkpoint sorts those traps into a few questions you can ask of any surprising number.

cards.headline: Four questions for a surprising number
cards.body: Is it a mix? Combining groups can flip a trend, as at Berkeley. Was it an extreme? Extremes drift back toward average, so a fix applied at the worst moment looks like it worked. Is the group small, or were many things tested? Chance alone then throws up standouts and "significant" flukes. Who got through the filter, and were groups or people measured? A selected group, or a pattern across places, may not describe everyone, or you.

In each case the data tell you about the gate as much as about the world, so the fix is the same: ask who is missing.

title: What Big Data Can and Can't Do
objective: After this level you can explain why huge amounts of data still mislead when they are biased, using Google Flu Trends.
summary: Google Flu Trends read flu from searches, but many matching searches just tracked winter, so it guessed too high for years. Big data should add to careful data, not replace it.

cards.headline: In 2013, Google's flu tracker saw more than double the flu the CDC did.
cards.body: It was built from Google searches, a mountain of data. It still missed, week after week. Why a mountain of data can point the wrong way is this level's lesson.

cards.headline: Reading the flu from searches
cards.body: Google Flu Trends began in 2008 with a simple bet: when flu spreads, flu-related searches rise, so counting searches might track the illness. To build it, engineers sifted about 50 million search terms for the ones whose ups and downs best matched the CDC's flu records. No clinic visits, no lab tests: just the patterns in what people typed.

cards.headline: Part flu detector, part winter detector
cards.body: With 50 million terms to pick from, some matched the flu season by coincidence. Searches about high school basketball, for one, rise with winter, and Google's developers had to weed out terms like that. Researchers who studied the tool called it "part flu detector, part winter detector". It missed the 2009 pandemic, which didn't follow the winter pattern, and from August 2011 it guessed too high in 100 of 108 weeks. By February 2013 its estimate of flu doctor visits was more than double the CDC's.

cards.fact: Big data works best as a supplement, not a substitute.
cards.context: The researchers named the mistake "big data hubris": assuming a giant new data set can replace traditional data collection instead of adding to it. When they combined Google's numbers with the CDC's delayed reports, the mix beat either one alone. In 2015 Google stopped publishing its own flu estimates and shared its data with researchers, including the CDC. More data isn't better data if it measures the wrong thing.

title: A/B Tests: Experiments on You
objective: After this level you can explain how apps and websites run randomized experiments on their users and what those tests can show.
summary: An A/B test randomly splits users between two versions. Bing found a 12% revenue gain this way, yet most tested ideas fail, and a test answers only the question its numbers ask.

cards.headline: An ignored Bing idea turned out to be worth over $100 million a year.
cards.body: In 2012 a Microsoft employee suggested changing how Bing showed ad headlines. It was cheap to build but ranked low priority, so it waited more than six months. Then an engineer simply tested it on real users.

cards.headline: How an A/B test works
cards.body: Version A is what users already get: the control. Version B has one change. Each user is randomly assigned to one version, and then the numbers are compared. Because chance, not the user, decides who sees what, a clear difference points to the change itself. Bing's test found the new headlines raised revenue by 12%, more than $100 million a year in the US alone.

cards.headline: Most bright ideas fail
cards.body: Microsoft, Amazon, Booking.com, Facebook and Google each run more than 10,000 of these experiments a year. The humbling result: at Google and Bing, only about 10% to 20% of experiments produce a positive result. Across Microsoft, about a third of ideas help, a third do nothing and a third make things worse. Even experts often misjudge which is which. That's exactly why they test.

cards.fact: A test only answers the question its numbers ask.
cards.context: Bing found that worse search results make people search more and click more ads, so both numbers rise. Those gains wouldn't last: frustrated users would eventually switch to another search engine. An A/B test can show that a change moved a number. Choosing numbers that match the long-term goal is the hard part.

title: What "70% Chance of Rain" Means
objective: After this level you can explain what a forecast's percentage means and how a forecaster is checked for being well calibrated.
summary: A 70% chance of rain means at least 0.01 inch at your spot on about 7 days in 10 like this one, not a share of the area or the day. Good forecasters are calibrated.

cards.headline: The app says 70% chance of rain. Seventy percent of what?
cards.body: Of the day? Of the town? Of the forecaster's nerve? Chapter 1 taught you to ask "out of what?" A weather forecast has a precise answer.

cards.headline: A chance of rain at your spot
cards.body: The US National Weather Service defines it exactly: the chance that at least 0.01 inch of rain falls at a given point during the forecast period, usually 12 hours. So 70% says that on days like this one, your spot gets some rain about 7 times in 10. It says whether, not how much. A drizzle counts the same as a downpour.

mascot.line: People mix these up all the time. The percent is a chance at your spot, not a share of the map or the clock.

cards.headline: Not the area, not the hours
cards.body: It doesn't mean rain will cover 70% of the area, or fall for 70% of the day. Both are common misreadings. Behind the number, forecasters combine how confident they are that rain will form with how much of the area it would reach. But the answer is always a chance at a spot.

cards.fact: A good forecaster's 70% days are rainy about 70% of the time.
cards.context: That's how forecasts are checked. Gather every day a forecaster said 70% and count how many brought rain. If it's about 7 in 10, the forecasts are reliable, or well calibrated. The same should hold at every number: about half of all 50% days should be wet. A forecaster whose 70% days are mostly dry is crying wolf.

learned: Chance of at least 0.01 inch at your spot
Not a share of the area or the day
70% means rain about 7 days in 10
Calibrated: 70% days are rainy about 70% of the time

title: When the Favorite Loses
objective: After this level you can explain why a candidate given a 70% chance should still lose about 3 times in 10, and why that doesn't make the forecast wrong.
summary: A 70% favorite should lose about 3 times in 10. If favorites never lost, the forecasts would be too timid. One result can't prove a probability wrong; a long record can.

cards.headline: The forecast gave her a 70% chance. She lost. Was the forecast wrong?
cards.body: Picture an election forecast, with made-up numbers, that makes one candidate a clear favorite. On election night the underdog wins, and everyone says the forecasters blew it. Maybe they did. But one night can't tell you.

cards.headline: 70% for is 30% against
cards.body: A 70% chance of winning is a 30% chance of losing: 30 in every 100 races like this one, or about 3 in 10. As one forecasting guide puts it, a 75% chance means that 25 times out of 100, the opposite is expected to happen. In Level 7's terms, 30% is close to 1 in 3. A 1 in 3 chance is far from rare.

cards.headline: If favorites never lost, that would be the problem
cards.body: Remember calibration from Level 93? Across all the races a forecaster calls at 70%, the favorite should win about 7 in 10 and lose about 3 in 10. If every one of those favorites won, the forecaster wasn't brilliant, just too timid: they should have said higher than 70%. Upsets, in the right amount, are what honest forecasts look like.

cards.fact: One result can't prove a probability right or wrong.
cards.context: Unless a forecast said 0% or 100%, either outcome was allowed. A forecaster is judged over many forecasts, not one night: do their 70% calls come true about 70% of the time? So when a favorite loses, the fair question isn't "Were they wrong?" It's "How often do their 70%s come true?"

cards.headline: Upsets: expected

A 70% favorite loses about 3 times in 10
If favorites never lost, the forecast was too timid
Judge forecasters by their record, not one night

title: When Algorithms Get It Wrong
objective: After this level you can explain the trade-off between false alarms and misses in a prediction algorithm, and why bias in its data carries through.
summary: Algorithms trade false alarms against misses. COMPAS shows two fairness tests that can't both be met; Amazon's hiring tool shows biased data carrying through.

cards.headline: Every spam filter makes two kinds of mistakes. Shrinking one grows the other.
cards.body: Some junk slips into your inbox; some real mail lands in spam. Any algorithm that sorts things into yes and no faces the same trade-off, and it matters most when the thing being sorted is a person.

mascot.line: Keep this pair straight: a false positive is a false alarm, a false negative is a miss.

cards.headline: False alarms and misses
cards.body: A false positive is a false alarm: a real email sent to spam. A false negative is a miss: spam let into your inbox. The filter scores each email, and anything above a threshold counts as spam. Raise the threshold and you get fewer false alarms but more misses; lower it and the reverse. Where to set it is a choice about which mistake hurts more.

cards.headline: Two fair-sounding tests, one algorithm
cards.body: COMPAS scores how likely a defendant is to reoffend. In 2016 ProPublica studied it in Broward County, Florida: Black defendants who did not reoffend were nearly twice as likely as white ones to be labeled higher risk, 45% against 23%. Northpointe, its maker, replied that the scores predicted reoffending about equally well for both groups. Computer scientists then proved that, except in special cases, no risk score can meet all these fairness tests at once.

cards.fact: An algorithm learns the patterns in its data, including the unfair ones.
cards.context: Amazon built a tool to rate job applicants, trained on 10 years of résumés sent to the company, most of them from men. It learned to mark down résumés containing the word "women's". Amazon lost confidence that the tool was neutral and scrapped it. Bias in the data carries straight through to the answers.

cards.headline: Algorithms: weighed
learned: False positive: a false alarm. False negative: a miss
Moving the threshold trades one for the other
COMPAS: two fairness tests that can't both be met
Biased training data gives biased answers

title: Reading a Health Headline
objective: After this level you can check a health headline by asking about absolute risk, the study's design and its size.
summary: Check a health headline with three questions: the real numbers per 1,000 (processed meat: about 56 vs 66 bowel cancers), the kind of study, and how much evidence there is.

cards.headline: In 2015, processed meat joined tobacco in the WHO's top cancer group.
cards.body: Ham, hot dogs and sausages, filed alongside cigarettes. The headlines wrote themselves. Three questions turn a scary headline into something you can judge: how big is the risk in real numbers, what kind of study found it, and how much evidence is there?

cards.headline: Question 1: how many people, out of how many?
cards.body: The WHO's cancer agency said each 50 gram portion of processed meat eaten daily raises the risk of bowel cancer by 18%. Eighteen percent of what? Cancer Research UK turned it into people. Out of 1,000 people who eat the least processed meat, about 56 get bowel cancer in their lifetime. Out of 1,000 who eat the most, about 66. That's 10 more per 1,000: real, and much smaller than it sounds.

cards.headline: Question 2: what kind of study?
cards.body: The strongest evidence came from large cohort studies. These don't assign anyone a diet; they follow people over time and watch what happens. And the top group measures how sure experts are that something can cause cancer, not how much. Smoking raises lung cancer risk about 20 times. Same group, very different sizes.

cards.fact: Question 3: more than 800 studies, reviewed by 22 experts from 10 countries.
cards.context: That's the opposite of one small study making a splash. So for any health headline, ask all three: the numbers per 1,000, the kind of study, and how much evidence stands behind it. Here the answers were a real but modest risk, from watching studies, backed by a mountain of research.

learned: Ask for the numbers per 1,000
18% more meant about 56 becoming 66 per 1,000
Cohort studies watch; they don't assign
The top group means sure, not big

title: Two Ways to Count Crime
objective: After this level you can explain why police records and victim surveys give different crime numbers and what each misses.
summary: Police records count only crimes reported to them. The victim survey asks people directly, finds fewer than half of violent crimes reported, but can't count murders.

cards.headline: Ask how much crime there is, and the US government gives two answers.
cards.body: One count comes from police records, the other from asking people directly. They don't match, and they aren't meant to. Each catches crimes the other misses.

cards.headline: Count 1: crimes reported to police
cards.body: The FBI's Uniform Crime Reporting program, begun in 1929, gathers crimes reported to law enforcement agencies, with counts down to cities and towns. It's local and detailed. But it can only count what reaches the police. A stolen bike nobody reports never makes it into the numbers.

cards.headline: Count 2: ask the people
cards.body: The National Crime Victimization Survey, run since 1973, asks about 240,000 people age 12 or older, in about 150,000 households, whether they were victims of crime, reported or not. In 2024 it found about 23 violent victimizations per 1,000 people, but only about 11 per 1,000 were reported to police. Fewer than half ever reached the first count.

cards.fact: The survey can't count murders.
cards.context: It relies on interviews with victims, so homicide is out, and so are crimes against businesses. Police records catch those, but miss everything unreported. Neither is the true number on its own. Together they give a fuller picture.

Victim survey: asks people, reported or not
Fewer than half of violent crimes are reported
The survey can't count murders
